The Directors Manchester Trust Limited, recognis- ing the need of other facilities than those already afforded for the investment of money by way of deposit, have decided to Rive special attention to this class of usiness, and have taken suitable premises at No. 73, King-st., Manchester, for the puroose. They ii ye accordingly arranged the system of secarity set forth in the following. One of the principal features of the system they have devised is the establishment by trust deed of Specific Trust Fund, whereby, independently of Vie credit and resources of the Manchester Trust it elf, with its sub cribed capital of £500,000 and reserves, securities at least equal to the amount of the deposits must always be held absolutely charged as security to the depositors. The security thus obtained is of an absolute character, and constitutes for the depositor an insured and guaranteed in- vestment. both as to capital and income, free trom all market fluctuations pnd Niche:twice.
The depositors I each fund will be secured (First ly).—By a first charge upon the securities lodged in Le fund. (Secondly). —By the guarantee of the Manchester Trust • ited.

One of these funds will comprise mortgage securities only. Investors in mortgage securities, instead of seeking for separate properties, upon which to lend their capital on mortgage, may deposit their money in this fund. The ad- vantages to be obtained are—Freedom from individual risk, any incidental failure of security being spread over a large aggreg ,te or wortgages, and. in addition, the guarantee of the mortgage by the Manchester Trust Limited, both as to principal and interest. This guaran,ee, at the present time, is the business of Mortgage insurance Companies, but the necessity for it wdl be obviated by this much more convenient system. When the money has to be returned there is no un- certainty, trouble, or delay in repayment. Borrower, also will find numerous advantages, mole par- ticularly in the fact that the private necessities of lenders wil, not interfere with the permanency of th, mortgage. Tie general aim of the Manchester Trust Limited in mak- ing these arrangements is to provide for the wants of the numerous investors of mnderate as well as of large amounts of savings accumulated beyond the limits of the saViags banks and oi investers who like to have their capital at occa- sional command. and who obj-et to have it absolutely locked up and out of their control for indefinite periods,
Dated 14th d.ty of April, 1892.

CAPITAL" CHAT:
The club gossips aay that the Duchess of Albany contemplates a second marriage. An English peer ismentioned a 4 the happy man.

-- At a meeting of anti-Parnellite raembers held recently a report was received from Dr. lux with regard to his American tour, and a diechision took - -place as to the arrangements to be made for the general election. In the end it was, I understand, decided that the party should contest not all, but practically all the seats now held by Mr,John Red- mond and his friends.

The Church party are trying to get up a new agitation against free education, and the Rev. Wal- ter R. Smith, the reactionist vicar of Corton, seems to have chosen himself as the leader of the move- ment. He sends a letter to the "Pies," from which, by reading between the lines, we gather that the abolition of fees is:telling-already on the Church schools, and that the si.becriptions are shrinking.

Tom Mann has been beaten in what may be called the final heat for the general secretaryship of the Amalgamated. Society of Engineers. One day Ander- son and another day Mann was at the head of the pall, and the increased excitement and energy to which these fluctuations led reintroduced for the moment some of the thrilling charms of the old sys- tem of open voting in Parliamentary eleetions.

Mr. R. L. Garner is still, apparently, bating no jot of heart cr hope in the matter of Mastering , the language of nadhkeys_ A Simian dictionary appears, however, not to be yet in view, for Mr ' Games methods are laborious, lie is now, he announces, preparing a ne* series of very novel experiments embracing msny sounds of the human voice of monkeys, birds. machines, and musical in- struments. So far he has found no intrinsic differ- ence between the vocal sounds of man and simian. Their voices differ in compass, pitcu, and flexion, but not in their "mode of propagation," whatever that may mean.

What is known as the most beautiful book in the world, that is,".The Book of IC,AIs," preserved in the library at Dublin, is ah )ut to be reproduced in facsimile. It is a manuscript of the eighth century containing the tour Gospels in Latin.including pro- logues. The pages of this highly valuable MS. are almost entirely covered with ornaments. The initial letters of every senteacb in the Gospels are treated as a subject, and this with amazing variety. In the facsimile no attempt will be made to reproduce the colour—because the attempts hitherto made in this direction have invoriably proved failures—but by the use of isochromatic 'method the proper balance of light and shade can be to some extent preserved.

According to a foreign correspondent, the Emperor of Germany is an ardent musician, He solaces himself of an evening with music.and draws somewhat liberally upon the virtuosi of Berlin. At his after-dinner chamber concerts he altogetherlays aside his stiff, haug'siy bsaring, and is geniality it- self to the musicians who have been summoned to play before him. He is art enthusiastic Wagnerite, but hi a admiration for the composer of " Loben- grin" does not altogether flow from, an artistic motive. The Emperor is'aparriot in his music as in everything eise. He reveres Wagner for the rea- son that lie-was the tone poet °tithe grand national legends and a stout ivatiottalist. die dislikes Italian music, and will not, if he can help it, listen to a bar of Rossini or the other Italian composers:

The Empress is a fairly skilled violinist, and will often play at die after-diuner concert's. 'The Emper- or has his gift in a very pleasant baritone voice, which he is not unwilling to lift in song. But as a rule both he and the Empress are content to listen in appreciative silence until half-past eleven comes, wheulhe inusic is hushed, and the imperial party retires to rest,.

The newly-formea Anti-Tobaeco League, which has Dix' Drysdale as its preSident, will no doubt'be stirred up,to redoubled efforts, by the Chancellor of the. Excheqiier's . announcement that the use of "the noxious weed " is op the ity'rease, and his suggestion that the tv,ze ot the habitual smokers is diminishing. Nlosi jih win admit that it is in- jurious ,ior growing loy,, to p:tiloke,.and the use of tobacco by women has. very few supporters. But the attempt to get up a per y in fiivour ofstbe legis- lative prohibition of smoking is doomed to failure, for Sir Wilfrib Lawson and his friends are far too astute to think of tasking on tobacco to alcohol as a subject for prohibition or . local option, and in re•any gonstii tient:les' the votes of tobacconists and their cusforners lire 00 nun:emus for anymindidate -to go out of his wss i i !!ite %11C111.

People came and people went from three o'clock to nearly seven in good-humoured and decidedly admiring Shoals. Mr. Bigelow is able to give some interesting part intik!, of Mt. Edison's latest researches as noted during a recent vi-it to the inventor's house. Mr. Edison do, s .not despair of being one day ,able to frighten microbes, out of our lungs with electric currents and undercurrents, for it is known that besides requiring a certain condition. of external ! ',surroundings they are extremely senaitiVe, and therefore easily aff-cted. Mr. Bigelow describes Mr. fiiiimort's storehou4e of materials as comprising ' samples of eery ,-uhstance ever used or likely to be used by man,' which have been gathered toget- her at a cost of about forty thousand pounds. As an exati4e of the practical utility of these exten- sive resources,it is noted that. before the right carbon for the incandescent amp was discovered, it proved necessary to experiment with a large number of substances; until the thing wanted was found In bamboo from North Japan. Mr. Edison declares that when he wants young men to train 'as assist- ants, he finds his best material, not in "college bred " young gentlemen, but in the ragged boys of New York, who are "quick-witted, anxious to move up, and will do anything to get along." "The best stuff I have here," he said. " is pure American meaning lads with two generations of American training behind tlient

The Brazilian Minister in London states that he has received the following despatch from the Minister of Foreign affairs at Rio datei on Monday. " A seditious movement ha-ring been promoted by some Anarchists under pretence of a manitestotion to celebrate Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca's restoration to health, the Govern- ment took prompt and energetic measures, thus frust- rating this attempt to disturb public order, Subse- quentiv some members of Congress who enjoy immunit- ies having been known to be involved in the seditious movement. the Government, in order that &flimsy be punished, has proclaimed the state of seige during three days, in accordance with Articles 48 and 80 of the fed- eral constitution. div.head: WH.A I.LEY FRAUDS. SENTENCE ON HAYDOCK. . _ _
div.p: THE WH.A I.LEY FRAUDS. SENTENCE ON HAYDOCK. . _ _

On Saturday, in the Crown do-nit-, -St. Oeorge's Hall, before Lord Coleridge, ES3II Ha vdock, chief clerk to the late Henry S. Whalley, s. or, Southport and Blackburn, was pot forward to receive sentence. Haydock, who is 37 years of age, was eighteen years in the employ of Whalley, and he was indicted on eight counts charging him with having conspired with his late employer, and by means of fraudulent devices obtained sums of money from several persons with intent to defraud and cheat them of the same. 'Upon one of these counts, viz., that of having conspired with Whalley to obt tin £650 from John Clieveley, an innkeeper, living near Chorley, the prisoner was found guilty by a jury on Friday even- ing. Upon hearing the, verdict counsel for the Crown ' intimated that he would offer rico evidence as to the other charges. His Lordship said the prisoner was clearly convicted of an ingenious and elaborai a fraud, and he felt that the prisoner must have known what Whalley was about. Be would take into consideration the recommendation of the jury, and sentence him, not to penal servitude, which he would otherwise have done, but to nine months' im- prisonment.

div.head: REPRESENTATION OF ROSSENDAIE.
div.p: THE REPRESENTATION OF ROSSENDAIE.

In reply to an invitation by the Rossendale Liberal Executive, Mr. Maden, M P., has consented to again allow his name to be suhmitted to the council. The Unionists,while declaring their determination to fight the division at the tvxt election, have not yet secured a can- didate. Sir Thomas Brooks has twice declined, but a still further effort is to he made to secure his candidature.

lilt. GEORGE•WHITELtY AND HIS CON-

NECTION WITH THE LIQUOR TRADE. The tollowing letters deal with a point of some importance, and will be read witb interest : 12, Bold-st., Runcorn, April 6th, 1892. Dear Sir,—ln the report of your speech delivered at Northwich, on Saturday last, the following sen- tences occur :—" Of one thing he (Mr. Brunner; felt very well satisfied, and that was that Mr. George Whiteley was going to behave as a gentleman, and the Liberals woull*behave like gentlem n to him. They would fight him as hard as any man ever was fought—but he was perfectly satisfied that neither Mr.Wbiteley, nor he (Mr. Brunner) nor any one else would his below the belt."

"Mr. Whiteley very modestly put aside in his candidature, during a recent speech, all connection with the liquor trade; but they might depend upon it, that it was because of his intimate connection with the liquor trade that Ye had come to Northwich." The enclosed is (as you will see),a short summary of a speech deliveted by Mr. Whiteley at Wincham, taken from last Friday's paper. In it you will see that he gives an emphatic denial to the assertion made as to his connection with the liquor trade. This speech was made two days previous to your own. Are we to conclude that you had never heard or seen anything of it? Or,if you had, how are the two quotations from your speech to be reconciled? Yours, very truly, WILLIAM COB. _ _ _

---- J. T. Brunner, Eq., M.P. Extract from Mr. Whiteley's speech at Wincham, on the 30th March :—"He contradicted the statement which had been circulated, that he was connected with the brewing trade. Be had no interest indthat trade, either directly or indirectly." ,
MR. BRUNNER'S REPLY. Druid's Cross, Bth April, 1892.

Dear Sir,—Your favour of the 6th has this morn- ing come into my hands. Mr. Whiteley...is the son- in-law of a brewer. Now, if my son-in-law tried to obtain votes on the strength of a declaration that he "had no interest " in the alkali trade "either directly or indirectly," I should feel bound to usk him to "draw it mild and blow the froth off." Yours truly, JOHN T. BRUNNHE. Mr. William Coe.

div.head: AN " OI7LD IRISH GINTLEMAN."
div.p: AN " OI7LD IRISH GINTLEMAN."

"A real (mild Irish gintleman," of O'Connell's slay, Dillon Browne, having drunk away a tine pioperty, found himself in the streets of Dublin without a penny, without a friend, an I without character or the credit by which he might borrow a penny from a friend, if he had had one remaining. How quench the drunkard's imperative thirst ? Having re-olved and rejected a hundred wild expedients, he at last 1 hit upon one of some promise. He hurried away to the house of an undertaker who was celebrated in that day in Dublin for the excellent sherry with which he regaled his customers. He knocked at the door with one tremulous hand, while the other held a handkerchief to his face to hide his unmanly tears. Ushered into the undertaker's sombre par- lour, he gave way to that emotion which he had to master in the heartless streets. He broke down so utterly that the undertaker—a soothing than—all undertakers are soothing men—tried in vain to as- certain even the nature of the bereavement which prostrated him thus. At last the professional angel of consolation bethought him of his famous sherry sea restorative sv hien had seldom' failed in such cases. He hurried away, to return soon with a de- canter and glass. The mourner was induced to try the restorative; but still every time he tried to speak he broke down; ana every time he brokedown he seized the decanter and poured himself out another glass of ,the tonic. When he bad drained the decanter.dry—that is, when most men would have become inarticulate—he found voice enough to say only: "Spare no expense; I want you to provide everything--everything." Here, as though tearful of another unmanly break-down,he hastened from the room to the hallsdoor,pursued by the sym- pathetic undertaker. "But., my good sir, my dear sir, the deceased—the deceased—th e corpse ? " " Oh provide that tco I" cried Brown, cheerily; as he bolted.—" The Correspondence of O'Connell."

div.head: PETTICOATS FIRST WORN BY MEN.
div.p: PETTICOATS FIRST WORN BY MEN.

It is a remarkable fact that the petticoat was first worn by men, and that even in this age and generation men are loth to discard its filvving dra- pery. I like to ' record this fact, writes a lady. Naturally, women take a sort of savage satisfaction in discussing a weakness in the 'Other aex,. especi- ally in the matter ot dress. Please don't stare me ()tad countenance at the supposed presumption of my assertion .that men have, or appear to have,.a sort of envious feeling toward us for having stolen from them this prerogative, and that they chltch at every means in their power to wrest it from or at least slfare it with u7S, for I'll prove it before get through. And we do not Wonder that this is so. There is dignity in drapery, as well as greed and wlegance. Ween Henry VIII, went to meet Anne of Cleve, s he was habited, we read "in a coat of vel- vet, somewhat made like a frocke, embroidered all over with flatted gold otdamaske, with small lace mixed between, of the same gold, and other laces of the same going traversewise, that the ground. little appeared ; and in a description, of a sitni- Aar gafment b,ioit_iu.4. to his tai- her, Henry VII., we read ol its being decorated with' bows of rihhoris,, quite as a belle of .the present day would adorn a ballroom dress. It is well known that the garment was at first not alone a skirt, but, ,as the name detiote,, a little coat. Mow it came to lose its upper half or body we do flat know, unless the "petticoat" was made with long skirts for the sake of the warmth, and in each case it was as much a petticoat, as we understand it, as anything else. We have only to look at Shaksperian characters— nay, let us be thorough, and go back to the time of the patriarchs to discover the skirts of men. And ettslly eeough we trace them ilovin. thronah the trues. Id the inventory of t lo3.eff-cts,of Inry: appears " ..)etticOat. of red dame 4k ' open sleeves,' end althraigh it was a question whether this had been fashioned for a man or ,woman, it wohld, if a woman's, be the only instance known More' Elizabeth's time of a woman using auch a garment, Thus we.bear nOlbing of women's coats hefore the Twit* period. '• Good Queen4less,'• with all her learning, which watt essentially tnascit- line in her dge and time, had the true instineta jf womanliness in her as regalds personal adornment, arid even though we find Cer deficient its taste, and heartily wish she had not made such a guy of her- `self in her old age, yet as ft *Oman We have her to thank for stockings and petticoats and many other luxuries which have tcerne necessities, and which we new L_ppreciate with as true a belief in our in- alienable right totheir sole possesion as though the right.had fallen to us from Mother Eve instead of Maiden Elizabeth.

div.head: AN ADVENTURE IN THE AUSTRALIAN
div.p: AN ADVENTURE IN THE AUSTRALIAN
BUSH.

Mr. F. H. Grundy and his friend, is Mr. Phillips, were in Australia, sojourning at a little inn tin the bush. Soon after their arrival they were invited to dine the next day at the house of a neighbouring " squatter," who liv,cl on the other side of a small river. That night it rainedireavily. The river was unfordable, hut at one place a good-sized tree spanned it. The trunk was elippery al, er the rain, but the two Englishmen crossed safely, and had a delighi tel evening with their host and his hopit- ! table wife. Mr. Grundy gives toe following account of their subs( quent experiences:. When the time came for returning, we began to think rather her- vously of the river. The night was pitch dark, and a drizzling rain had set in. We arrived at the' river hank, but could not find the log,and wandered about discon,olately. At last vge struck it, and in my pleasure at our good luck I stepped carelessly upon it, smoking my cigar the while. Suddenli 1 slipped—into the foaming torrent ? Not quite that, but very near it. lied it been so, nothing could have given me a chance. I had arrived at a forked branch, and the main tree suddenly thinning, I had trodden too much on one . side. Fortunately, 1 was able to catch the smaller branch. There I hung, feet and legs in the water. I made seve- ral attempts. to regain the log, and then began to see my great danger. I almost. lay upon the water, holding fast to the branch,'arel calling loudly to Phillips to come and help me. For answer !received shouts Of laughter—hysterical, I dare say, but not reassuring. By a last, great effort—and I knew it was the last—l got one leg over the smaller branch; then, after resting a while in comparcive security, I got upon the log and crawled to shore. When there I found that I. had my cigar still alight be- . tween my teeth. I was safe, but my cabbage tree hat was gone. Mr. Phillips was no longer laugh- ing;' he was much more nearly crying. He " dared not come over alone," and implored me to come and help him. Never a word l answered; but marched, off to the inn. Phillips arrived the next morning with a bad cold, but no word ever passed between Us concerning that adventure. That night I was a sort of hero at the public house. Much was said about ray adventure, and when tlie loss of my hat was mentioned, a black Fprvant, who was stone blind, and to whom I had given tobacco,spoke up quietly,"! suppose him at Cropked Nos 4 Bend," and was seen to slip out of the room. Crooked Nose Bend, I found, was half a mile or so down the river,and no one could tell why blind ,lackey had hit Upon the place. Nevertheless he' presently re- turned with the hat! "Me get him in a minute," he said, as if the feat were nothing to speak of. To me it seemed almost a miracle.

14" At the Liverpool AsAires, on Tuesday, before Lord ' Chief Justice Coleridge, John Hylands (20), pleaded guilty to unlawfully administering a nosious•drug to Louisa Jane Hutchinson, it Widnes, on August 8. Prisoner sobbed very bitterly, and hid his face during the whole of the time he was in the dock. Mr. Segar, who defended, stated that the drug was not actually administered, as the girl put it out of her mouth immediately. Prisoner had done what he could for the girl since the last Asslzes, and he had always borne a good character. . . .

_ His Lordship said prisoner had pleaded guilty to what under certain circumstances was an extremely serious offence. Fortunately, in this case, but little harm had been done. Prisoner had borne a very good characrer previously' and he was apparently very penitent for what he had done. If he really was penitent he would have an opporiamitv of making the only amends which an honourable man would make in such a case. The

prosecutrix herself strongly recommended prisoner to mercy, and his lordship desired to give him another ells nce. He would, therefore; hind him over in three sureties, himself for £lOO snd two sureties of £25 each, to cstne up for sentence when called upon.

div.head: QUEEN AT HYERES.
div.p: THE QUEEN AT HYERES.

flrEnas, TIIZSDAY.—The statement that her Majesty intended visiting Lord Salisbury is without foundation. The Queen never intended to pay such a visit. The pro- bable visit of the Prince of Wales was announced tor the 13th of this month, hut it is almost certain that he will not come in the entourage of fie Queen. It is whispered that this is because there are no suitable apartments at liberty in the. Royal residence ; and that those vacated by the Duke and Duchess of Connaught have been already promised.
TtIE MURDER Tllli-WIWI A BROKEN. OFF WEDDING. A POLICE-SERGEANT SHOT DEAD.

Sergeant Moulden, of the Wilts constabulary, was shot dead on Tuesday by Lewis Hamilton, who is wanted for the Melksh,an murder. . The first murder arose from ill feeling towards his victim, Richards, the uncle of a girl mimed Fhrsnee Adatns, to whom ilamilton was engage :I to be married. The banns were published in Sr. James's Church, Devizes; on the 3rd inst., tau:. the girl, acting, it is a llegei, on the advice or Richards, subsequently broke off the match. This greatly enraged Hamilton; who threatened to murder the girl and her relations, a threat which he has. partly. carried intryterrible effect. Later inguities show that Hamilton's real hamo is John Grind, and that his parents live at Shaftesbury:- He is about 30 years of age, and WAS employed as attend- ant at the county lunatic asylum, where Miss Adams was also engaged as housemaid. The murderer was dis- charged from the asylum on Tuesday week, And it appears that this was the point at which relatives corn- ' menced to show their Opposition to the marriage.

. Superintendent Perreft" With • three other officer,' were • searching for the prisoner between Coattley and War- : minster very early on Tuesday morning, when they met him a few miles from the latter place. Hamilton I accosted the superintentle.nt, saying, " Do you want me : sir ?" then instantly striptiing back he put his baud to his pocket and took out the revolver. Superintendent Perrett grappled with him and pushed him back against a bank by the roadside' and Sergt. Moulde,p and the other constables rushed to their chief's assistance. Hamil- ton, however, was. too (pick for them, and levelling his pistol fired twice. The first shot missed, but the second struck Moulden just below the herirt,'and he fell dying into the arms of his comrades. Constable Langley wrested the revolver front the prisoner and handcuffed him. He was then removed to Warminster lock up. Five cartrideca fiot the revolver were found on I him. He admitted having ' shot Richards, his sweet- , heart's uncle, at Melksham, and said that if he could have found theyoung woman he would ,havei killed her too, fie said also that he had been trying to elude ar- rest since the first murder. It has been ascertained that he was in Bath on Sunday. He called about ten o'clock on Monday night at an inn at Corsley and asked for liquor. Being refused, he shot a horse in the neck that was t•therecl outside the inn and made off. It seams that it was in conseqoence of information given to the War- minster police about this affair that they started in pur- suit of the man, whose description agreed with that of the murderer of Mr. Richards.. Sergeant Moulden had only been at Warminster two months, having pr.:l./misty been stationed at Shrewton, a village on Salisbury Plain. He leave,, a widow and four children. REMARKABLE LE fTER FROM THE PRISONER. At the inquest the only witneas called was Florence Adams, who stated that she wrote Gurd declining to !have anything further told° with him in coneequence of I.his.bad reputation..- 'She heard that whiliit' he was an attendant at the asylum he borrowed money from pati- ents and others, The hanns of marriage were published a second time, and then they were withdrawn. On Sunday last she received the following letter from the accused:—" My dear Flo,—Please forgive me tor taking the liberty of writing to you heain, but do please read this before you throw it into the fire. Oh, my dear, I am broken-hearted, and-have sent to ask your forgive- ness. My dear,! know that lam guilty, but it is through you Fin, my dear, that I was in such difficulties. You know, Flo, my dear, or at least you must think, that it • has cost me a lot of money to do as I have, when I have been out with you. Now, dear Flo, that lam ruined you look on me with scorn, but never mind when I can I will return tio Devizes and pay every penny, and follow you to the end of the world,- I will have bitter revenge some day, first on you and your old neople or some one. Take notice of this for I mean it, that is if you give me up. But, oh, Flo darling, do please forgive me for the wrong I have done you; and don't get married just yet. Give me time, piri dear, to get over this and pay what I owe. I will Pay every penny When I can. Indeed I will, my dear Flo, if you will only have Mercy on me. Do ask Harry (the murdered Ame.le) and dad to think of me as well as they can, for if any poor wretch was in need of their pity! am. I have done no crime, and only owe sonie money which I will pay as soon as I can. Lam go- ing to America. Now, dear, don't tell where lam go- ing, mV dear, I mean not to the police. For the sake of better times fknow you will not, my dear. I will take care of the ring until we meet again, and I know we shall some day, and then if you are a wife you shall die. P.S.-0i), my dear, have' mercy on me, and don't get married." The letter closed with three crosses, representing kisses.

div.head: !IL
div.p: !IL
' (Als, Rums REsrAvisto.) THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS;
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN, • Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "Where the North Wind Blows," tke., eke.
CHAPTER XXXIL TIIE SMUGGLER'S SIGNAL.

" Three lights abreist. The two end 'uns to be kept steady, but the middlemost to gan backards an' forrads, like the light in a boat ov a stormy neet.. Ye'll mind that yon's the signal, lads, an' if the coast's clear, make for Frenchman's Bay forst." Bill Widdrington was to be in command of the Bonny Bess for this voyage • while his iather-in- law, whose rheumatism forbade him from venturing to sea at that time, was to manage affairs on land. All was hurry and confusion on board the sloop, though in a subdued sort of way. Men ran hither and thither, preparing ropes and sails, and storing away empty casks and stores in the hold; while others kept a strict watch ashore, lest a sudden raid of the revenue men should take them unawares. As old Carr, standing near where the boats were busy, gave the crew necessary information with regard to the signal, which was changed every voyage, as a precaution against treachery, he for- got to keep his voice down to the proper pitch. Suddenly, to his great consternation, a small figure rose from the rocks, close beside him, and sauntered up in a cool and unconcerned manner. I am very sorry gentlemen, I am, indeed, 'pon : my honour! I have unfortunately overhead your words, and so perhaps you had better change your signal. Though, of course, as a gentleman and a man of honour, I—Hell and fury ! What is the meaning of this outrage?" Before finishing his elaborately polite explana- tion, Mr. Wynne was seized upon by two burly sailors, and held firmly between them with his arms pinioned to his sides. "Oh, come, now, I protest against such treatment," said the poor man; indignantly, " I relied upon your sense of justice, I did indeed !. Mr. Carr, Bill Widdrington, all of you—surely you won't let me come to harm because I was too honourable to hold my tongue." " What on earth are we te de wiv the blatherin' fyule ?" growled old Carr, with half-amused, half- angry, perplexity. One of the men who were guarding Teddy—a coarse, brutal-looking fellow— grinned, and then drew his hand across his throat with a significant gesture. Bill Widdrington strode up immediately, and wrenching him from his hold on the caPtive, sent him staggering backwards. " Aw'm d—d if ye shall touch him?" he swore with vigour • then gloomily added hat there was blood enough on their hands already, and that it would be queer if a curse did not on its account follew, them wherever they went. _

After the first disagreeable surprise of findmil fcks where he had expected friends, Teddy awaitec his fate,with great composure. There was no want of courage about him, and he would have thought it exceedingly bad breeding to appear too anxiout about his own life.- , Ile fumbled with the hand noli left free, thanks to Bill's intervention, for his eye- glass, and fixing it, regarded the blood-thirsty sailor with a calm and critical gaze; a gaze which had tbe effect of completely disconcerting that gen- tleman, and at last drawing from him a savage enquiry as to why the devil he was to be stared out of countenance by a weazen-faced monkey like that, whom he could eat for supper without pepper and salt, and feel none the worse on it. . ,

"'bon t be too sure of the latter fact, my ferocious friend," 'replied Teddy, with ready impudence, " I rather fancy 1 might disagree with you. I am quite sure that my last prayer would be a pious one that Providence might so order it, for the sake of poetic retribution."
Not understanding badinage, the sailor retired from the line of vision, sulky hut abashed. "What on earth are we te de wiv him ?" repeated old Carr.

" Aw canna tell, unless we take him along with us !" replied Bill, and this suggestion was carried unanimously, much to Teddy's disgust. To think of it! To think of that consummate exquisite having to rough it in a smuggling sloop, along with a set oi ill-conditioned ruffians, who would think nothing of pitching him overboard if he offended against any of their prejudices; a thing which, ignorant of the said prejudices, he might easily do, ruffians who knew little of the virtues of soap and other toilet requisites, and smelt of tar and bilge water. .Of the danger of the expedition, Teddy did not think much, but of the unpleasantness a good deal. • He would have to live with them, eat with them, per- haps—horror on horror—even sleep with them. These thoughts did seriously oppress the poor little man, and cause hini to hang his head in a very disconsolate manner.

_ . "Cheer ill), Air. Wynne," said Bill Widdrington, with one of his old glints of fun, "Tom Dodds shanna eat ye while we've a bit o salt junk aboord." "But to go for .an indefinite period, and without even a change of linen. It is too shocking," mur- mured Teddy, lugubriously, "and then my sister —what will Lady Callerley think?. Poor Silvia ! She is a nervous little creature nowadays, seems to have fits of the megrims often. She will fret her- self ill if she is left in ignorance of my fate." There was genuine aindety in these last words, and they touched Bill in a tender place. Family affection is the most sacred of things amongst the fisherfolk. Bill considered a little. •

_ " Aw'll manage that, Mr. Wynne,. if yell leave it to me. There's a message goin' te Bell by a safe hand, and if ye'll just scribble a line, she'll deliver it hersel ; as for the linen, yell ha' to make shift te de wivout it, till we get ower the water where yell find yersel' i' the land o' plenty.'' Teddy found rather a difficulty in wording his communication; because upon, subgaitting the first written one to Bill, it was peremptorily set aside as telling too much. , "It's not that aw misdoubt ye, Mr. Teddy," whispered Bill, "but them cheps is -as keen as hawks, an' one darena' leave them a clue Aw've never had the command o' th' Bonny Bess afore, but wor best man, Dick Daglish, is under a cloud, an' has had to flee ower the border wiv a price on his heid. An' for what he never had no hand in, not he, canny man! An' them 'at's guilty ganuin' free, mebbe—gannin' free, but not happy—hoo can they ever be happy with blood on their hands, and blood not sheil in fair fight either." • Teddy looked at Bill iu surprise. The fisherman's eyes were fixed on vacancy, his hands worked ner- vously, and he talked in a wild, disjointed manner, utterly incomprehensible to his hearers. " Ah, yes, I heard something of it. The murder of poor Lanes, you mean? You speak as though you know, or at least had some suspicion, of the one who is really guilty, eh ?" Bill recovered his composure, and put on a dogged inpenetrable look. . . • .

'Me ? Hoo sh,puld aw knaw owt about it ? Aw was only tellin' ye hoo it tame roond that ma sted 'o Dick w,es skipper this trip, an' that's why aw feels 'sponsible like.. Just you pencil yer bit message, an' gie it te me at once, for time's up, an' we men be off An' if ye'll take ma advice, Mr. Wynne, ye'll mind yar own business, an' not fash yer heid about what disn't consarn ye, 'specially aboord free-trader; 'cause the skipper's word's la*, mind that hinny, when he rides the waves on his own ship." At last the letter was written and met with ap- probation; and soon the Bonny Bess was pitching about, in a manner more lively than pleasant, on her way to the coast of France. Near shore, where the cliffs afforded shelter, it was quiet and calm as a mill pond, and Teddy congratulated himself upon having gained his sea legs very readily. • As he swaggered about on deck, with his hat cocked-rakishly over one eye he began to give him- self airs, and to think that it was not such.bad fuzi after all: And then the adventures he would be able to recount when he returned! Why he would . .
-- - be quite a hero L Eve Bell would be forced W admire him.

But Tom Dodds, the sailor whom he had discom- fited so mightilSi* grinned a sardonic grin in passing; knowing well that time brings about its revenges, and that a strong westerly breeze, the very breeza they wanted to blow them across cannily, awaited them out by. Alas, for the poor little dandy's sea loge! They did not stand hnn in good stead when the sloop be- gan to jerk from the summit of a mounta.nous wave to the deep valley lying between it and the one that followed close upon its heels. The noise was like that of a perpetual cannonading, and at each suc- cessive assault every plank and mast seemed to groan and shriek out a noisy remonstrance. The Bonny Bess was a seaworthy little sloop, ,and was used to worse we...ther than this in an ordinary way, but then, unfortunately for him, Mr. Wynne was net. He looked at the sky, where not a star was visible, and at the sea, where the salt scud flew whitely in the darkness, and he wished himself sale ashore. What a fool he had been ever to let these cruel bloodthirsty wretches know of his presence ! it be lived to set foot on dry land once more, which war exceedingly doubtful at ore-sent, catch him be.ng 80

puileunous unuer Like cauumatakces again. dust as he had come to this noble conclusion a huge wave struck the sloop, and sweeping over the deck, knocked him down and nearly washed him over-. board into the bargain. From this untimely fate he was rescued in the nick of time by the skipper, Bill, and handed over to the tender mercies of that inember.of the crew who acted as cook and steward, to he carefully- s.owed away below, out of danger.
nAr-rER XXXII'. A 6ALE IN SEPTEMBER.

As the time for the, return of the Bonny Beal drew near, the weather changed considerably for the worse. The wind, veering round with audit= sweeps to.eastward, promised mad doings. It is only just to say that his is the sort of proinise it ' never fails Alison that bleak and inhospitable coast ' to fulfil. The fisher-folk—more especially those who had either a share in the smuggling sloop or a relative on board of her—grew exceedingly anxious, and with keen prophetic 'Vision watched the signs of the heavens; deciding that these looked more ominous of storm, than their wishes for the. safety of the sloop would have liked to see. Day after day the clouds gathered and lowered portentously, and the sun hid himself behind a ve.l of mists; though occasionally, just at the period of his down setting, a sickly yellow gleam pierced through the leaden masses that lay along the western horizon, and, with a lurid, but transient illumination lit up the miles of black throbbing water. Restless, and for ever on the wing, the gulls flew inland; or screaming scudded over the heads of persons walking along the shore. • Upon one afternoon in particular the'gale gathered strength, and threatened to break all bounds. By this time the sea waarwining extremely high, and a white line of breakers was broadening fast. Everywhere-Is/ma sound of rush and of confusion; of muttering and roaring, as though the elements were gathering their forces of war, and were yelling i out their battle cries up aloft. Huge balls of foam rolled over and over w th bewildering rapidity, or whistled through the air, until they dispersed themselves into space. Bell Widdrington, standing by the door of her cottage, peering with eager vision across the field of foam, notien:l a brig in great distresi making southward, probably trying for the port of the Tyne. The fisher, girl doubted much if the poor vessel would be able to reach it, since it was in such a crippled condition. This increased considerably her anxiety about the Benny Bess. • Besides the danger from the troubled sea, the revenue cutter had been sighted cruising about the coast diming the previous day; and if Bill knew of its vicinity, he would most probably dare all rather than fall into its clutches.

Sincerely Bell hoped that the ship she was in- terested in`would—if not already snugly sheltered in some more southerly bay—keep well out to sea. As the evening drew near, the gale increased; and the foixe of the wind blew the pretty waving .hair ci the fisher girl backward, holding it there as tghtl as though it were grasped by a human hand; while she, setting her lace steadily towards the east, continued her vigil. . Immediately bcneath—a brawling current rushed Yarrop hurn—rnshed, on in Mad eagerness' to meet /Ltd grapple with the brea:mrs On the shoe ; Where its noisy music was speedily overborne and lost amid the 'Magnificent 'thunderous bass of the angry ocean.

To Bell's Rionsiderable astonishment, when she at length turned landward rho saw a horse, riddec by 'a woman's figure, struggling bravely over the top .of the ilow bank on the opposite side of the water; and evidently making for the ricketty wooden bridge, there to cross the burn. The fore:: of the gale seas condearated here, blowing with terrific force down the gully as into the mouth of a funnel; and it seemed once or twice as though the poor beast and its rider must of a certainty be overturned. , Whoever eould'be mad enongh to venture out in such weather, and on horseback, too? Bell won- dered. Why it looked' like—but no, that was- surely impgssible, Yes, it was indeed Lady Caller- ley—the silly; misguided, venturesome bit lassie ! She reached the bridge at last, and, waved her riding whip towards Bell, in gay defiance of the weather.

Bell held her breath as she watched the progress. She had always had her doubts about that crazy bridge. It tottered and shook under the horse's feet, for its foundations were being sorely tried by the spate ; but for this one time it held good. Bell ran to meet the horse, and led it up to the door; panting and limping, poor creature, as well it might, after its great and heavy exertions. In a moment Lady Gallerley had alighted, and stood in a sheltered 'place in the lee of the house; patting and caressing her favourite. "Good pet, dear good old Britomart, you have done bravely by your mistress, and she will not for.- get you for it! Quick, .Bell; let us stable her, and .give her a drink; for she certainly needs a rest greatly." "But, my lady How 'cOmes it that ye're out by "yersel, on such a fleet too. Whaur's Sir Lancelot that he let's ye gan on in this fond fashion ?" "Tut, tut, my child. Ask me no questions until we have attended to Britomart's wants! Well for me that have learnt to.saddle and bridle my steed myself; thanks to that funny old squire and his head groom tOo,iether. Give me a whip of stray,- now to rub her down with. Gently' Witty,. gently old lass! it isn't every day you nre groomed by a lady, you know.'• • Bell srhiled to see how deftly the bonny little lady performed a grgom's functiolls. She herself did not know much about horses, and could only give very clumsy help. If it had been a boat now! Nobody could beat her at managing and looking after that. At length the mare was made comfortable; and Lady Callerley condescended to enter the house and to wash her hands.

There she found, old Nanny.; looking smaller and crosser and older than ever, an effect that was pro. bably owing to the east wind; and in the thorough mood of a prophetess. • " VThatten a blast's blown ye this way, my leddy ?" she asked, querulously, " Ye're like the kittiwakes and the pee-wits, that love to be astir' when storm, bad luck, an' misfortunes are i' the air!"

"That's a poor welcome, Nanny," replied Silvia, laughing, and shaking the wet out of her curls, as she knelt before thefire ; "do you not remember that I have a brother on the sea just now, anShave a right and reason to be anxious 1" "A brother! Ha' ye a brother 7" asked Nanny, pretending ignorance; then when Bell rethinded her that it was Mr. Wynne who had made her a present of, the warm shawl she had on at that moment; she gave a sniff, meant to express unmiti- gated contempt for the gift and the giver. "Oh, aye, aw maist forgot, that yon Frenchified bit of anatomy was kin te ye. An' yet aw might ha' kenned, for the pair on ye wad only make a decent sized body atwixt and atween ye. An' whatever , Sir Lancelot was thinking on when he slighted a fine woman like Madam for sneji--" _ _

"That'll dee granny,noo, none C.' yer fond clash !" interrupted Bell, hastily, " but ye winna mindher, ma leddy, her bark s waur nor her bite, an' she's put cot aboot wor Bill forbye ! He's her favourite, an' she's fair set on. him, ye knaw." "Oh, I know her thoroughly by this time, so you need make no excuses, Bell, said Lady Caller- ley, laughing again, "She's always borne me a grudge for entering this wonderful Callerley family, where everyone ought to be strong and gloomy like —well, like my husband, there Now, don't try to appear shocked or surprisecl my girl; because you are not either at heart, you know. Gracious ! How wet my hair is ! The air is completely saturated with salt spray all the way from here to Seaton Callerley !" " Ye'll catch cold, ma' bonny bird," remarked Bell, in an anxious tone. "Where is your hat, Lady Silvia ?" "Gone Flown away miles inland by this time, I should say, judging from the rate it travelled, after it left my head. Good riddance too--great heavy ugly clumsy thing. Hats are only a nuisance in a gale of wind. I shall adopt your fashion in future, Bell, and tie a shawl over my head When the fit is on me to wander abroad on stormy nights." "It never ought to have taken ye. Aw'll warrant Sir Lancelot knows nowt o' yer carrys on, this time." Silvia drew up her tiny figure and frowned. "Why do you harp on about Sir 'Lancelot for ever and ever? What cares he where I am, -so long as I do not trouble him about my doings? He has been, and still is, out alone. Am I to eat my heart out in solitude because he chooses to leave me to my own devices? It is great fun to steal away from home like this, with no one—not even a groom, to tell the secret of where I am. Bell, that is not all, dear, that is not all the truth ! I heard in a round-about way from one of the kitchen maids that the Bonny Bess was expected to-night. I want my Teddy, oh, Bell, dear, I want my brother ! the only creature on earth that loves me and—and that needs me ! Surely God will not take him from me also ! I kr* nix baby—my prat-, soft, dimpled,

Nanny shook her head, : and muttered to herself in lugubrious accents. " Ay, ay, that's rest! land were the same as those used in regard to Ireland now. The very language that was used was the same. ' Separatist," "disruptionist," "unprincipled agitators," "Rome Rule," " mob rule;" and all those expressions and arguments that were cast up int their teeth at Ihe present day were used half a century ago in Newfound- land. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) ?diss Gornall then sang" When the heart is young." Dr. R. H. TODD, in the course otan interesting adtress, ridiculed the assertion that the Irish people Were seek- ing separation from England. They did not intend to be guilty of any such insane folly, and, he asked, sup- posed they attempted to do it were they to sweep the British armies from the land, and the Britisa fleets from the water with their blackthorns ? (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He bad to tell them that Irishmen were not foolish enough to separate tbeinaelves from the great advantage/sof the connection with England:' Irishmen had taken part in building up the British etnpire just as much as Englishmen and Scotchmen had, and they were not going to be so foolish as to throw aside that great inheritance. (Hear. hear.) Referring to the Ittempts to stir up religious passions in Ulster, he said Meer was pointed to as the great difficulty in the way of Home Rule, but he asked them not to be deceived by these statements. If the people of Ulster gathered in their masses of their own spontaneous motion and said they would not have Home Rule there would be some force in it. But what was the fact ? Ulster returned a majority of Home Rule repre.entatives at the present moment, and Ulster had had no mass meetings. (Hear, hear.) It was proposed by the Tory wireptillers to have a mass meeting of 10,000 people in Bet last to protest against Home Rule, but they should remember that Belfast itself contained 300,000 people and Ulster con- tained upwards of 1,000,000. Three great railways ter- minated in Belfast and it was proposed to have excursion trains on a holiday, and two of the members of Belfast, whoowned large shipbuilding yards, were going to gists their workmen a holiday and turn them out in procession in thh street, and this vast gathering of holiday people was to be called a great demonstration against Home Rule. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He asked them to.' to take note ef how this gathering was got up, ant also of the fact that Ulster returned a majority of members against Home Rule, (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mrs. Houma)* then gave a song, and on being loudly encored rendered " The oil folks at home." Mr. STRINGIER moved, and Mr. Adams seconded a vote of thanks to the speakers and singers and also to Miss Fleming for playing the accompaniments. This proposal was supported by Mr. W. Pierpoint and carried with acclamation. The CHAIRMAN having returned thanks the meeting terminated. MONDAY.—IN BRICK-ST. SCHOOL.

On Monday evening the reception was held in the Briek-st. Schoolroom, and there was again a very large attendance. The room was crowded, and the utmost enthusiasm again prevailed. Councillor J. 11. Fleming presided, and there were also present Mr. C. Furness, M.P., for West Hartlepool ; Dr. and Mrs. Houston, Mr. W. Pierpoint, Councillor 11. and Mrs. Roberts, Mr. W. 'Jeffrey, Mt. C. J. Holmes, Dr. Gornall, Mrs. Loughlin, Mrs. and Miss Cavanagh, and Miss Fleming. . Ths CHAIRMAN said he was quite sure that when they , had heard Dr. Houston they would be quite satisfied ! that be was the right man to represent Warrington. By his opponents he was called a foreigner, but that was cruel. Mr. Wl:red Pierpoint was as much a foreigner as was Dr. Houston. He was born in Warrington, but that was about all he (the chairman) knew about him. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) They would no doubt nay that he (the chairman) was a foreigner, but .Ithough he had lived in Warrington only lOyears he vefitured to say that the people of Warrington knew, a little about him. (Elear,hear.) Lord Salisbury had said that the Irish were Hottentots, but he asked them to look at Dr. and Mrs. Houston and say if they were Hottentots. (Flear,haar,and laughter.) Why Dr. Houston should be called a Hottentot he could not tell, because it was generally supposecrthat Ireland was nart 01 the United Kingdom. (Hear, hear.) They were also told that they were Separatists, but he denied that they were anything of the kind. What they wanted was a union of hearts, and until they got that there could be no peace in England. (Heals hear.) When they got rid of the Irish question they should he , able to get on with English questions, and those ques- tions Dr. Houston understood as well as he understood I the Irish question. (Hear, hear.) When Dr. Houston got to Parliament, and he (the Cnairman) felt sure he would get there, he would show them the way they could be represented. Up to that moment they had been misrepresented, but they would not be any longer, and he urged them to make up their minds to fight that brdtle as if it were a fight to the death. (Loud applause.) Mrs. Houston then sang "I must away," for which she received a most enthusiastic encore. Mr, B. H. Pearson accompanied the song on the iohin.• ' Dr. Elousems, who was received with enthuiastic applause, and on the call of the Chairman,an additional three cheers for the Doctor and his wife, said the Chair- man had alluded that night to the only point,he thought, 'that had been made against him on the other side, and that was they said he was a foreigner. (A Voice r "Never mind 'em," and loud laughter and applause.) Well, if he wa4 he thought he was in the process of be- ing naturalised in Warrineton—(applause)—and he thought that at the next general election his naturalise tion would be complete. (Renewed applause.) He had now traversed a large portion of that great constituency, and met the electors face to face; and he was satisfied from what he had learnt in that campaign that the elec- torate of Warrington had determined to put an end to that mischievous Tory denomination which for the last seven years had left Warrington without any real repre, sentation in the counsels of the British Empire.(Applause.) The elector; had a great and serious responsibility cast upon them, a ateeponi bilks. and a duty, which they owed not simply to their friende and supporters hut to every elector, every inhabitant of the place. (Hear, hear.) Their duty to their friends and supporters was to select a marl who would maintain their political views and support their plaice! interests, but their duty both to their partisans and to their opponents was to select a man who would promote those intereets which were above and beyond the mere interests of party: (Applause.) The Liberal organisa- tion of that borough had faithfully discharged its duty, • but he did say that upon the last two occasions, not to go further back. the Conservative organlsatien in the borough had lamentably failed indeed. The effect of it had been that they had allowed their action to be dictated by personal, and what he might call historical considerations, with the result that Warrington had been represented in the imperial Parliament by a figure-head. (Applause.) He did not Want te say a word against one of their fellow citizens' especially as he was in the even- lag of his life, hut he did say,this, that Ule people by sending to the House of Commons a man who was either ! unable or unwilling to discharge his Parliamentary duties as their representative ought to have discharged them, had incurred a very grave responsibility. (Applausa.) And new the Conservatives asked them again to trust to their choice and to accept their nominee. What guarantee had the electors of Warrington that their choice would be more wisely exercised now than it 'had been upon the occasions to which he had , referred ? What guarantee had they that the man the I Tories had selected would more judiciously or effectually I attend to his Parliamentary duties than his predecessor I in the high office, when his predecessor, Sir Gilbert , Greenall, failed? He could not see that any such ! guarantee existed. No argument that he could per- ! ceive had been out forward in the case of his opponent that for a moment could be accepted as sufficient or satisfactory. It was most irnplrtant at the present day that a representative in Parliament should be a real and active and working representative, and that not merely In the interest of any political party, or section of the community, because it. was manifest that at the present day a number of qaestions were de- cided and debated and a number of divi- sions taken not upon mere party lines at all He would take a question thit occurred upon a very re- cent occasion—of the exemption of machinery from taxation. rhat was a question which affected the in- interests of people, no matter whether they were Tories, Liberals, or Liberal Unionists, and that question was discussed, and the decision upon it took place perfectly irrespective of any question of party or politics at all. And he said that ',the vital interests of the nation de- pended upon the election of a man whom they could rely upon having in his place when a question of that kind came up. Warrington had a great future—he was happy to 61v—before it—(applause)—it was increasing in numbers and in wealth, and was advancing in im- portance, and could not afford to Ir,se the advantage which the constituency of a norough p‘isse3sed by being represented in Parliament by a man who would watch its interests. (Hear, hear.) Therefore, whether the elector was a Tory, a Liberal, cr I something between the two, which was called a I Liberal Unionist,he was equally interested in the matter Ihe was bringing before the meeting, lie could not find that any valid argument had been laid before the electors in support of the Candidature of his opponent. It was stated that a member of the family had been favourahly known for the support given by her ,to the institutions of the town. He said all honour to her for that. (Ap- plause.) He should lie the last person in the world who would seek to detract be one single' iota from the credit that should attach to her for her, benevolent exertions in the place. (Hear, hear.) But,en the other hand, could it be said for a moment that Mr. Robert Pierpoint was en- titled to a single particle of credit for it? (" Not a bit.") Why, you might as well attribute a knowledge of music to a man because his brother played the German flute. (Applause and laughter.) It rather showed that oppor- tunities had been missed by Mr. Robert Pierpoint than it showed any interest taken in the town by that gentleman (Applause.) If that argument and the argument that he was a foreigner were left out of the case, he did not ' see what reason could be brought forward why Mr. ! Robert Pinpoint should represent Warrington. Suppo.."- lug they passed by that, let them ask themselves for t moment, if Mr. Pierpoint was returned to Parliament. wljat would be do there ? (. aVtahing," and laughter.)

div.p: THE EX AIiIINERiI SATURDA Y , • APRIL 16. 1891, •

Where was his programme? Why did he not tell them ? (A Voice " He is going to borrow it from Sir Gilbert Greenall," and laughter) The Liberals had published theirs. It might, he read in evereespeetCh delivered from their platforme. He need not go over it that night, but the first plank in it, as he had said over and °seer and over again, on every Liberal platform was Home Rule and justice for Ireland. (Loud applause.) He was glad to see that the question of its relation to the workmen of the country was thoroughly understood in Warrington.. (Hear, hear.) Dr, Houston read the following letter he had received froma working-man, who had he been a professor of political economy in the oldest university in the three kingdoms. could not have put the question, mere clearly and distinctly than he had done :—" Sir, excuse my writing to yeti, but be ng a working-man, I venture to ask the question, will Rome Rule benefit the working-men ?To my mind it will do, through the labour market. The labour 'market is greatly overstocked as the result of evictions in Ireland. ((lear, hear.) Irish- men have been driven from their homes and the land of their birth to seek employment where it was to he found. They have not all had sufficient of this world's Wealth to take them across the sea to the land of the free. Therefore a large portion of them have sought and ob- tained employment as farm labourers around here, and have taken the places of our own farm labourers who have been compelled to seek employment in the town. Thus, there have have been more labourers than can be employed. AS the result, wages have been reduced from 'a pound to 17e. or Mi. a week. Should we, sir, give Ireland Home Rule, naturally these Irishmen would go back and re-take the farms or homesteads from which they have been evicted. This would reduce the labour market in the towns, as a farmer must have his la- bourere, even if he pays more wages, and many would go hack to an agricultural life for a little more wage. Thus the town's labour market would be left in a more Prosperous condition than it is at present." The speaker then cited other points in the Liberal programme, one man one Vote, reform of the registration law, of the housing of the working-lasses, the regulation of ground rents, mining royalties, and wey leaves, of the duration of Parliaments, Ice. He characterised the attitude of the Tory party towards democracy as distrust tempered with fear, and that of the Liberal party towards it as trust tempered by prudence. He concluded by saying that the Tories had got one foot in the grave and the other upon the edge of it—(laughter)—and they would very soon tlimble in altogether, and would ith very decently and completely interred, under a mound of ballot papers ; and he should be greatly surprised if a considerable contribution to these hullo, papers did not come from the people of Warrington. (Loud and con- tinued applause.) , ' Mr. C. Fuurtess then gave a recitation, " Dating a boot peck," in the Lancashire dialect, and it was highly enjoyed by the audience. Mr. C. FURNESS, M.P. for West Hartlepool, who was received with loud applause, then gave an address. He remarked that the constituency had been 'fortunate In securing the services of so able and eminent a politician as his friend, Dr. Houston. • (Applause.) He could never forget the able services which Dr. Houston rendered to him in his candidature a year ago in the Parliamentary borough of the Hartlepools, when they had a very keen contest there. (Applause.) Some time before that election took place they nad a visit from two very able gentlemen, one being Sir Charles Russell and the other Dr. Houston—(applause)—and he (Mr. Furness had been I able to trace from that visit that many who in 1888 were somewhat nervous in regard to Home Rule had been an thoroughly convinced by the very able speeches then delivered that he found when the election took place Chat they were amongst his ablest and strongest sup- porters. (Hoer, hear.) If they, at Hartlepool, could turn 1:000 minority into a majority for the Liberals of 300 what could not they the people of Warrington do? (Hear, hoer.) The con- ditions at Warrington were very similar to those at Hartlepool. The progress of Warrington was owing to the sturdy working-men of the constituency; and the progress of the Hartlepools was of a like kind, and he could not for the life of him believe that the workingmen of that constituency would longer follow the Tory party of privilege and monopoly which had always been opposed to giving power to the democracy of the country. (Ap- plause.) He was glad to hear of their theiellent pros- pects in Warrington. In travelling in the train that day he told a gentlhmen who was in the same carriage that he was going to Warrington. The gentleman remarked that he knew Warrington very well, and ha understood they were going to cnan,ge the representation of the town this time. (Hear, hear and applause.) Having referred to the broken pledges of the Tory party, he said the time had arrived when the Government would have to give an account of their doings to the people of the country, and he was persuaded that the result would be to give Mr. Gladstone their great leader—(applause)—his last chance. The Tories were often telling them to look at what good measures they had passed', but they never told them of the measures they had tried to pass ; they did not toll them, for instance, that they had tried to fix a tax on sugar, a commodity which housewives had to purchase every week. (Hear, hear.) The next Parliament would have to ' seriously grapple with the question of mining royalties. He had just travelled from the county of Durliam,which was suffering from a strike so severe as to paralyse the whole of the industrial community. The mine owners had had to reduce the price of coal for some months past, and they had requested the men to 'submit to a re- duction of wages but which they had refused to de. He maintained that if there was a sliding scale for royalties, and the mine owners had insisted upon a reduction in consequence of the reduction in the price of coals, the men would have been agreeable to take their share of the reduction—(hear, hear)—but when the whole burden had to he thrown upon the shoulders of the men they had resented that. (Applause.) If they had been in a position to deal with royalties, and wee-- leaves, he honestly believed the strike now taking place would have been averted.- (Hear, hear.) Those Were the questions with which they would have to deal in the future. (Hear, hear and applause.) He believed that the depression in trade at the present time was very largely due to the delay of the general election. 11. was himself largely engaged in the iron trade and in shipbuilding, and he found every day that people were holding back and would not give out orders, and, when asked the reason, they said they were going to wait until the general election had taken place. He said therefore that the sooner the general election took place the better it would be for both the toilers and the maim- fa,,turers of this country. (Hear, hear and applause.) With regard to Home Rule he most unhesitatingly said that it would benefit the working-men of England. In the shipyards with which he was connected they had got any amount of Irish labourers, and, having travelled as ' he had doae in Ireland and seen thousands of acres of land practically uncultivated, he maintained that those men who were in the habit of coming over to England for harvest work and who drifted into the towns, would be the drat to go back to Ireland after the passing of Home Rule. (Hear, hear.) He was delighted to find that their candidate was being abused. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) That was about the best sign tiny stranger like himself could have that they were going to win that election. (Applause.) They need care for no abuse: they wanted to carry the thing above personalities. (Hear, hear.) Liberal policy was to do unto others as you would have them do unto you. The chief end of Liberal principles was to give the greatest benefit to the greatest number. (Applause.) What were the principles of Toryism? To his mind they were summed up in about two lines :—" Whatever is, is right,' and "Leave things as they are." (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) He could not understand any working-class community being represented by a Tory. Although he had sat in Parliament for more than a year he had

never seen the member.for.Warrington, and he had not come across a member of Parliament who had seen the member for Warrington. (Laiighter and applause.) A growi'llg industrial town like Warrington could not afford to be nnrepresented. If it was there wonld be many things neglected which other boroughs similarly situated would have 'the advantage of. (Hear, hear.) They would be wise if they returned one who could lift up Ins voice and represent not only the interest of the borough of Warrington but also ef the whole country. (Loud applause.) . - Mrs. Houston next sang" Come live in my heart and pay no rent," and, being encored, she gave another mndering of "What Paddy gave the drum," a song which always gristly amuses the audience. Mr. W. JEFFRRY proposed a *cite of thanks to the friends who had taken part in the proceedings. , Mr. T. Manua, in seconding the proposal, said that according to statistics which he had in his hand, the roysltles on 600 tons of pig, iron amounted to about £2OO while the wages of 40 the workmen en- gaged in tne production of it, from the manager right dawn to the labourer, would only amount to about £95. (Flear, hear.) Ihe resolution was then put to the meeting and car- ried with acclamation.' _ _ _
Mr. .FIIIINKSS, M.P., responded, and Councillor El. Roberts having invited the assistance of all who wished to work for the return of Dr. Rouiton, the meeting ter- minated.

THURSDAY.—AT THE NATiGNAL SCHOOLS. Another Liberal reception was 'field at the National Schools, Church-st., on Thursday evening. The meeting was crowded. Mr. Joseph Mounfield presided, and there were also present on the platfqm r,--4)r. and Mrs. Houston, Mr. I. S. Leaden), the Liberal candidate for the Altrincham division," Councillors H. Roberts, Elem. ing, and A. Browne, Mr. W. Pierpoint, Mrs. O'Callaghan 'Mrs. and the Misses Fleming, Mrs. and Miss Gornall, and Mrs. Pierpoint. The Chairman in opening the proceedings, thanked the rector, and the trustees of the school —(applause)—for their courtesy in allowing the use of the school. (Applause.) Ile thought those present would think too that it was quite time, that they had a change in the represen- tation of that borough. They had been represented quite long enough by a silent member, and the time had come when they should have a man who would he able to represent their views and not those of the landed aristocracy of the country. It was little better than an insult to an important constituency like that, for they had been practically disfranchised for a long time; and in his opinion a man had no right to occupy a position when he was not able to fulfil the duties of it. They had in their candidate a gentleman they had every confidence in ; a candidate who was able to deal with the great questions of the day,that would come before the next Parliament. He (the chair- man) believed that if they got a Liberal government— which they were almost sure to do—there would he great Radical changes prepared ay the Government, and a man of ability and standing would be required to deal with them. They heard laet night that one of them would be the question of good government for London. There was also the question of royalties. (Aprlause.) Which was a very important matter to a constituency lien that, in which iron formed one of the staple indus— tries. He supposed that the royalties on a ton a ton of manufactured iron in this country amounted to about ss. 9d., while in France it was a little over 6.1., and in Germany very little more. France and Germany competed in the saninemarkets as England did, and if we had to compete with other nations' and maintain Ow proud position in Europe we csuld not aft n\d to be handicapped in this manner much longer. If in other countries only 61. per ton.royalty was charged while we charged ss. 9.1., the margin, since we were bound to sell at the same price, must come out of the blood and sinew of the working-men. After referring to the question of the death dues as one which would have to be dealt with, the speaker concluded by urging all present to do their utmost to promote the return of the Liberal candidate. Dr. Hoterrow, who was received with enthusiastic cheering, anal cheers also for Mrs. Houston, • returned thanks for the magnificent reception accorded to them in Warrington. (Applause.) They called him foreiener--(Laughter, and " Never mind what they call thee ")—that cry apparently had been drowned in the cry that had nightly rung in every hall where he had addressed a meeting. He came there to discuss with the people of Warrington the great questions some of which had been touched upon by the Cnairman, and he came moreover to preach the gospel of political peace and good-will between two nations. (Applause.) He was glad to say that he had found in Warriagton a disciple who could have taug'at the master, for he believed that in Warrington there were as good Home Rulers as were to be found in the four provinces of Ireland. (Cheers.) The gospel he Came to preach was not merely one of peace and good will, but one of prosperity and happiness to both countries. Tnat the existence of an Irish Parliament would be a cause of prosperity in Ireland there could be no doubt, became there was inure than a century ago a period of prosperity in Ireland which was unequalled in the annals of her history—in the period from 1782, when the independence of the Irish Parliament was recognised, down nearly to the end of the century when it was taken from her. Dr. Houston, in proof of this, read the testimony of Fitz‘ibbon, Earl of Clare, one of the traitors, he said, who helped to rob Ireland of her Parliament, and that of the Dublin bankers and mer- chants of the period. That showed he remarked, what could be done by a native Perliament--(epplatisel —and if that result flowed from that cause in 1782 why should it not flow from it in 1892. And the prosperity of Ireland had been put back now nearly a century by that cursed union which they were deter- mined to ge' rid of •• Like Mercy," Home Rule wenld not only bless Ireland who received it but also England who conferred it. (Hear,hear.) It was now too late in the day to say the Irish people were incapable of governing them4elves. He sometimes lost patience with the non- sense that was talked upon that question, but he was boond to say that he thought the people of Warrington understood that question very well, and they were not nicely to be misled by arguments which were either put forward at Tory meetings or in the literature which had been scattered in the constituency. He had seen some of it, and he tound that it made excellent pipe lights. (Laueleter.) That was the only light he had ever &Heed From the Tories. (Loud laughter.) He hid only one fear of the result of the election and that was of beer. (Hear, hear.) IF they were beaten at that election it would on t-e.er that would beat them and nothing else. He had been told that at. former elections in that constituency there were working-men found so dead to their own in- terests and so insensible to their duty that they sold their great birthright for a mess of pottage. (Hear. hear.) He hoped that times had changed to coins ex- tent, and he was happy that he thought the conditien of that fight had changed for the better. (Hear, hear.) But, with all the earnestness with which it was possible to preas a matter open them at a meeting, he begged and implored of them to cast \ out that plaaue from amonest them. (Hear, hear.) He could scarcely believe it possible that a man would barter that peat heritage, the fran- ehise,for as much beer as could be bought for a few cop- pers. It was had enough that the brewers should run away with so much of the hard earnings of the working- man and grew rat and rich upon it, hut it was too bad that they should rob them of their liberty and of the • weapon that had been put into their hands, after many a hard struggle by the Liberal party, for their defence. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that the workingmen of War- ringtnn at the election would take care that nothing of the kind occurred, but that when the election day was over every workingman in Warrington weuti be ahle to stay that he gave his vote as his conscience directed, and

he (Dr. Houston) far his part would respect the working- man who gave his vote against him when he conscienti- ously hPlieved he ought to do it. (Loud appl Mrs. Houston then sang "A Summer Night," and be, ing encored gave "Forget, forgive." The accompani- mentq were played by Mr. H. Bond on the violincello and Miss Fleming on the piano. Mr. I. S. LEADAM, who was loudly applauded, next addressed the meeting. He contrasted the conduct of. the two parties in the House of Commons with reglrd te working-class questions, instancing particularly the vot- ing that took place upenp Mr. Channing's motion as to the hours of railway servants. Mr. Howarth, a member of the Tory party, argued that these long hours were all right because labour was only a commodity, and in the • voting that took place only three out of the 124 who supported the motion were Tories, while 141 Tories voted against it. He also pointed to the hostility that had always been displayed to trade unionism by the Tory party', and commented upon the defects in the Employers' Llability Act. In the course of a very interesting speech,Mr.Leadam was frequently and heartily applauded. Mrs. HOUSTON then rendered another sang in a style which won an enthusiastic encore, when she gave the song "What Paddy gave the drum," the two last verses of which referred to the local contest and, which when sung, were loudly applauded. On the motion of Mr. J. Gandy, seconded by Mr. H. H. Dutton, and supported by Councillor A. Browne, a vote of thanks was passed to the Rector for allowing the use of the schoo's, and to the singers and speakers, and the Chairmaa. The Chairman having responded, the meeting terminated.
