div.head: SHIPPING DISASTER.
div.p: SHIPPING DISASTER.

• A telezram from Lloyd's azent at Stanley, Falkland Islands, dated March 21, arid received from Monte Video, on Monday, states that the British ship Viscount, from San Fransisco for Liverpool, has been totally wrecked. Three of the crew ilSincl*, Lincoln, and Reid), were drdweed. The remainder were landed at Stanley. ATTEMPTED MURDER.

Michael Mahon, who claims to be an American citizen, Was remanded at Heywood, on Monday, on a charge of attempting to murder John Edward Butterworth. The prisoner and prosecutor met on- Sunday night, when a quarrel respecting card-playing was renewed. Butter- worth struck Mahon who then, it was alleged, fired at him with a revolver.
MRS, OSBORNE'S PROBABLE RELEASE

div.head: FROM GAOL
div.p: FROM GAOL

The friends of Mrs. Osborne have received information which leads them confidently to expect that she will be released within thP next fortnight. Theprisoner's health is still such as to cause grave concern as to the results, mental and physical which would follow from her ac- couchement in gaol, and it is this consideration alone that has weighed with the authorities in determining the date of her release.
THE OUTRA.UE BY WIGAN COLLIERS.

At the Liverpool AFISIZeS. on Tuesday morning, Lord Chief Justice Coleridge sentenced Joeeph Moran aged twenty-six, collier, and John McGarr, found guilty of 4 shacking assault on Bridget Murray, at Wigan, on March 14. The prisoners were found guilty on evidence which was to the effect that the woman, a Factory opera- tive, was accosted by the men in Wigan. They then took her to a secluded street, and there committed the offence. His lordship sentenced, the prisoners to ten years' penal servitude. • MR. GLADSTONE AT HOME.

Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, accompanied by Miss Wick- ham, reached Chester railway station shortly after three o'clock on Tuesday afternoon from Euston. They tra- velled ip a special saloon carriage, and on arrivinif at Chester were recognised by a few persons on the plat- form. After a short deliy they left for Sandycroft by the Rhyl train. At fiandycroft station they were met by a carriage and driver, to the rectory at Flawarden, where they will remain for the Easter holidays. Mr. Gladstone is in robust health.

div.head: DAMAGE TO A VESSEL AT RUNCORN.
div.p: DAMAGE TO A VESSEL AT RUNCORN.

In the Nisi Prim Court., at Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, before Mr. Jastice Collins and a special jury, an action was brought by Henry J. Cooper, a master mariner, and John Meek,a tnerchant,against the Manchester Ship Canal Company to recover damages far injury to their vessel while on the de- lendents' gridiron at Runcorn. The defendants said that if there was any damage it was owing to the plaintiffs' action. Mr. Righam. Q.O. and Mr. Walton appeared fot the plaintiffs, and air. Gully, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. C. H. Russell for the defend ants. The wooden vessel Jenny Lind, built in 1850, at Virmouth, was purchased by the plain- tiff Cooper for £5OO early in 1890, She was of 157 tons register. She was to carry a cargo of coal to Rio Grande, and prior to her departure it was arranged that her bo•tom should b. coppered. She had been thoroughly repaired in 1887, and would have retained her class of Al at Lloyd's for nine rears; it would not have run out (intik 1898. Oil Juhe 16 she was entered for the Runcorn grid. When she was placed in the graving dock she lay to the pert side, about two feet from the quay wall. It was necessary to place her in the position to enable the men to get to the keel to do the work of cop- pering. On the following day it was found that two of the blOcks which supported the forward part of the ship had entirely gone, and for a distance of 21Ft. of the length of the vessel, the ship waa left unsupported. ' The result was that the vessel " hogged" or hint, and practically broke her back. The vessel afterwards went on her voyage and was lost off M trtiniqae. In Septetn- her, 1800, the plaintiff as:igned ilk claim to Meek for ' the sum of £3OO. Thee,ost of the repairs after the Run- corn accident came to £368, add there was also au amount claimed roc demurrage.— Mr. Golly said the de- fendants resisted the claim because they believed the action was an attempt to make them pay for the prac- tical rebuilding w the vessel—at any rate more than she cost a few weeks before the accident. HP peinted out that the action was not brought for 18 months after the accident and four months after the vessel was lost at Martinique. What the defendants said was that the vessel was a very rotten old ship, and had strained a good deal on her previous voyage, and was an extremely likely boat, unless carefully handled, to sustain damage if she was a lowed to lie over on , her bilge. They held that the plaintiffs had placed the vessel in an improper position. It was their ditty to examine the cridiion,and if the work could not hay been done to the Jenny Lind when in the position which he suggested she ought to have been in, the proper thing woulel have been to take her into a tire dack.—rip jury found for the plaintiff, damages £250, aid his lordship gave judgment.

Samuel LOTTAX, greeisgrocer. ankey Green, flied rather suddenly on Saturday morning, e bmit Sc' en o'clock, The deceased had not been yeell for sonie time. Mr. Lomax had (tarried on business at Sankey Green fora considerable period. Ile has left a widow and several children to mourn his loss. No inquest has been held. Ethel Geddes, aged eight weeks, infant daughter of Charles Geddes, engine driver, disci at about 4 a.m on Saturday somewhat suddenly. The deceased child had been sickly from birth,having had a fit when three weeks old. On Friday the family went to bed, and the child appeared to be all right. The next morning the mother noticed that it looked rather pale, and a few moments after it died in her arms. • Patrick Lennardy, 58 years of age, a labourer, who was employed at one of Messrs. Walker's breweries, died on Saturday afternoon, at half-past one. Deceased had suffered from bronchitis, but was able to continue at his work until the Wednesday evening, On Thursday morning he complained of a pain in his side. Various remedies were applied, and a doctor sent for, but Len- nerdy died at the time stated above. Nbinquest has been held in either case.

div.head: TIIE lIUDGET.
div.p: TIIE lIUDGET.

Mr. Goscrxxx as Chancellor of the Exchequer next brought forward his Budget. He said he had a surplus of £1,067,000 to show, but it was not due in any great extent La expansion of revenue. The Budget e4iinate of expenditure last year was £90,264,000, and the actual expenditure was £80,923,000. assisted edurat in, with the concomitant grants made to Scotland and Ireland, was put down in the Bidet at £923,000, but ultimately £1,006,000 had to be voted ; And while for Irish distress ithe Budget estimate was £125.000, £237.003 was voted. The total supplementary es'imatea were £660,000, brit the amount unexpended on the various services of the total grants was £998,000, showing a net saving of exs penditure of £336,0 0. as to the revenue of the year, Customs had produced £36,030 over the esti:nate, and this year " tobacco had been the feature, not alcohol." The increase from tea had been £150,030 and that from tobacco £418.000. He was sstry to see many little urchins becoming taxpayers as regarded tobacco at far too early an age. But there had not been in the past year that general rush to alcohol which had characterised previous 3ears. There had been an Inc, eased consumption of British sprite of 61 per cent, and of brandy of 5/ per cent, but beer had lagged behind, having produced £121,000 less than the estimate. Pile death duties had yielded an increase of £689,000, but the revenue from stamps had decreased £470,000, mainly in regard to City business." While he estimated an increase of £500,000 in income tax, and hoped to get £13,750,000, the ',urinate result was receipts I amounting to £13,850,000. Coming to the question of I the National Debt, the right hon, gentleman sad he put the reduction of capi: as liabilities for 1891-2 at £5,330,000 There had ts.eri also a deerea-re tri he fl atine; debt, mak- ing in the year a total diminution of £7,245,003. The total estimated expenditure for the present i4ir was £90,253,000, a net increase of £914,000. There was .an increase for education of .E1.477,C00. The total revenue he estimated at0.£.90.477,000. With his small margin lie propo:ed to make a reduction in patent fees and to provide for uniformity in the duty on sparkling wines. In concussion, Mr. Goschen spoke of the pro- Lability of the tariff arrangement, between Great Britain and Spain coming under revisor'. Mr. tiLADSTONIS followed after the formal motion re- lating to the tea duty had been put, and referred to the expansion and complication of the financial statement, partly in consequence of much that had taken place in recent legislation. He hoped the Chancedor of the Ex- chequer in any changes with respect to the wine duty would not confine his consideration to the effects in Spain, but also take into view any consequsnces that might he produced in other countries with which i Our commercial relations were more extended. In the pre- sent state of opinion on the Continent on the question of 'Protection and Free Trade the greate.t caution ought to be observed in bringing forward any measure at all likely to cause alarm amongst those interes's. Kr. Goscarrs, in reply, said no change was proposed in the allocation of the wine and spirit duties. As to the te- construetion of the income tax, it MIA too stupendous& task to undertake, at the end of a Parliamerit. He did not intend to fr.rget Mr. Gladstone's recommendations With re.gard to the wine duties. The first Ti irs lay after the ti,hdays he hoped would be set aside for the Budget pr0p.•)941. div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY APRIL 16, 1892.
TEAT the flowing tide is with the Houston

Liberal party throughout the coun- Warrington. try has been evident for several years. It is flowing as strongly at Warrington as elsewhere ; and may be said to have overflowed, on Wednesday night, when a second meeting in ' the Co-operative Hall had to be held to accommo- date the-crowds who were unable to fie.d seats or standing room in the Public Hall. All the old campaigners agree in saying that the enthusiasm of the Liberals of Warrington was never at a higher pitch. It is equal to, if it does not surpass, what was displayed in 1868 and 1880; and this means that a like result is to be expected—namely, that Warrington will be redeemed from bondage by the return of the Liberal candidate. Dr. HOUSTON has now made ten speeches in the borough; and such is his mastery of every phase of the political situation, and such is his skill in marshaling, his facts and arguments, that elec- tors who have listened to his addresses find him as fresh, as instructive, and as inspiring in his last speech as in his first. Let those of our readers who have not been able to attend the meetings judge for themselves from the reports which we give, this week, of the three "dditional Receptions, and of the magnificent demonstration of Wednesday night. Dr. HOUSTON. has been greatly assisted at these gatherings by' Mrs. HOUSTON, whose natural. gifts and high training as a vocalist have charmed all hearers. The Liberal candidate paid a well deserved compliment, on Wednesday,to the workers of ,the party,who, from the venerable President to the humblest membeib, are determined upon going from strength to strength and from victory to victory. But tb achieve this result, it will not do, as Dr. HOUSTON said, to depend entirely upon the machinery of the party. Electors who have made up their minds must canvass those who are doubtful. Working-men can canvass each other in the mill, the workshop, and the street; and ,he must be beyond redemption who cannot be made to see that, in the Liberal candidate, the masses have such an advocate of their cause—earnest, able, and just—as is rarely offered to any constituency. Dr. HotroN, on Wednesday,mercilessly exposed the sham loyalty of the Ulster party, who threaten to break the law if it is not made to suit therk and who are at the present moment plotting against the peace and unity of Ireland. He passed in review the various measures of the present Gov- ernment, which, he said, were for show and not use, and were the outcome of the political quackery which is the stock-in-trade of the Tory party. In the absence, through illness, of the Right Hon. S. Walker, \ attention afterwards centred upon Mr. Herbert GLAnsTonnt, who,' in an impor- tant and impressive speech, wade it clear to his Warrington audience that he is an undoubted chip of the old block. He hit the nail on the head wen he said that the Tory party had no pro_ gramme; whilst their one policy at the present moment was to oppose the Liberal programme. , Sketching the work which the Liberals had before them, he dealt point by point with Home Rule for Ireland,local government for London,reform of the registration laws, payment of members, one man one vote, shorter Parliaments, &c. In answer to those who were seeptical as to getting through so much work, he pointed to the splendid series of reforms which were carried out by the Liberal Government of 1869. And he might have added, they could still look to the Grand Old Man to ac- complish equally great things. The speech was one which will certainly' make Mr. HERBERT GLAD- STONE'S Vika to Warrington a pleasant memory. Mr. WILLIAM PIERTOINT presided at the ovee tolw d meeting, and struck the right note when h their the working-men that Dr. HousTo. was candidate, and that if they did the ir duty the result would be a- triumph alike for them and for Liberal principles. Taken together, the two. meet- ings deuionstrate that the Liberals of Warrington are eager and militant, and mean to win at the General Election.

Dr another column we publish a Has he an letter from a supporter of Mr. GEO. Interest ? WHITELEY, the Tory candidate for the Northwich Division, and Mr. BRUNNER'S reply. The important point xaised is whether Mr.
I

WHITELEY is interested in the liquor trade. Mr- BRIJ/ors& referred to him last week as having an interest, whereupon Mr. WILLIAM Con, of Run- corn, has written the member for the Northwich Division, drawing attention v. Mr. Warrntiftv• own statement to the effect that he has no inter- est in the trade "either directly or indirectly? Mr. Burman's reply is characteristic and condo- sive. He says :—" Mr. WHITELEY is the law of of a brewer. Now, if my son-in-law had trisst to obtain votes on the strength of a declaration that he had no interest in the Alkali trade, either directly or indirectly' I should feel bound to ask,him to draw it mild and blow the froth oft.'" Mr. Cos, after this, will, we imagine, ho sorry he spoke. He has got more than a Boland for his Oliver. But Mr. Brunner might have car- ried the matter even further. Our neutral con- temporary in the puff preliminary which it gave. the Tories" ingogoeigenetu:w.hofoheastphreoieniimseodnteoy,grcivae thdeaii; kn3wn not only that Mr. WHITELY Was the son- in-law of a.brewer, but that Mrs. WHITELEY wo an only daughter. What is the inference ? WIT that, in the ordinary course of nature, Mrs- - will inherit the brewer's accumulatea wealth and large interest in the Blackburn brewer'. In face of this how care Mr. WHITELEY say he hrgs' no interest "directly or indirectly' in the liquo/6 trade t He may try to brazen it out, but nov that the cat is out of the bag, will even Mr. William Coe accept the statement without sornethinf more than the proverbial grain of salt in 'order to` help it down? The Tory candidate evidently sigh.' —to use a sporting phrase—to run with the hazy. and hunt with the hounds; but be too far committed. At a recent public dinner , a Licensed Victuallers' Ass*ciation at BlackPoelr where tb" ' one of those scenes of ghastly festivity unfortunate tenants of tied houses are inviteil to cheer for their "owners," Mr. Wurrianv sta from the chair that it would be " his business' in the Nortbwich Division to defend the ieterests of the trade." As we had occasion the other week to comment on the report—which proves to be wholly inacurf Cte—that the late Mr. Spurgeon had left over £20,000, we gladly make room for the following statement, which places the matter in its true light "That Mr. Spurgeon might have died leaving ten times, aye, or even twenty times, as much wealth to cis widow, had the accumulation of wealth been his object in life, is an undisputed question; but all those who know anything of him are well aware that the heaping up of wealth was not his object in life. No doubt, under tne circumstances, Mrs. Spurgeon has acted wisely in affording the explana- tion that the £ll,OOO at which Mr. Spurgeon 's will was proved is inclusive of the estimated value of his copyrights, furniture, and a life policy for £l,OOO. Apart from this, Mr. ,':,purgeon died worth only £2,000. There are always some persons on the out- look for justice in others, though, perchance, they may not posses the remotest iota of that quality themselves, and no doubt a few of these foolish ones had been drawing ridiculous contrasts between the wills of Cardinal Manning and Mr. Spurgeon. Therefore we are glad that Mrs. Spurgeon saw fit to make the above explanation. Certainly the great Baptist preacher could not well have left less as a decent provision for his widow."

DRATX OiN a FORMER RUNCORN ECTIOOLMARTOR. 'lntelligence has just reached Runcorn of the death of Mr. James Lightfoot, son-in-law of the late Mr, Thos. Norman, of this town, at Craddock, Cape Colony. The .deceased gentleman for some years was headmaster of theltrunswick Wesleyan School, Runcorn, which posi- tion he filled with credit. He -was very highly respected in this neighbourhood. "The Midland News and iiarreo Farmer," in Craddock,Cape Colony, referring to the sub- ject, said Mr. Lightfoot wi,s horn at Idle, near Bradford, Yorkshire, in 1841. He received his scholastic train- ing at Westminster College, London. From there he was appointed diead-inaster of the public school, Runcorn, Cheshire, where he remained some years. Afterwards he was appointed head- master cif the Wesleyan School, Kentish Town, London, and his ?health failing him, he was compelled to leave England,. and come to the Colony. He accepted the appointment of head-master of the Heald Town Training Institution for natives, which he held for seven years. The climate pot being suitable to his special ailment, he was recommended to reside in Craddock, and two years ago he settled amongst us. Since then he took over the elementary school, conducted by the Misses Pilbrook, and has brought it to its 'present high standard of pro- ficiency. Mr. Lightfoot was a fully certificated master of the Department of Public Education, England, and held a Sonth Kensington Science . and Art certificate. We shall all miss Mr. Lightfoot and his influence in the town, especially over the young people, ‘and his loss will long be felt. To Mrs. Lightfoot we extend our heartfelt sympathies in this her boor of trouble.

ALLEGED BREACH OF CONTEACT.

In the Nizzi Prins Court, at the Liverpool Assizes on Saturday, before Mr. Justice- Collins and a jury, the Compagnie de Boles, importers of copper ore, Paris sued V. illiam Roberts. copper smelter, St. Helens, for damages for non-acceptance of a cargo of copper. The cargo did not Teach Garston till the 18th December, when defendant refused ue- livery, on the grounds that the: ore had not been tendered within a reasonable time. The claim was, therefore, for the difference between the original contract price and that actually paid. Before the finish of the plaintiff's case, the parties agreed upon terms,ivhich gave plaintiffs £250 damages.—His Lordship gave judgment for this amount. Sarirrr BICTCLES.--7. S. Garland, 51, Bridge-et., War- rington. See advertisement on page 4. NARROW ESCAPE AT EARLESTOWN STATION.

A man named William Mem had a vet}, narrow escape from losing his life at Earlestown Statii.n, on Saturday night. Diem and several friends had been to St. Helens, and returned to Earleatown by the train due at 1050. After alighting from the train he proceeded'along the platform towards the level crossing at the flaydock line, but by some means he fell between the carriages ot the train. which had just started for Manchester. An, alarm was given and the train immediately stopped, but on making a search, Irlam was found sitting on the opposite platform, bleeding from the head. How be got from under the wheels the man cannot explain, but the passengers on the platform expected nothing less than to hear that he had beea either maimed or killed. UMBRELLAS RECOTLEED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Bankey-at., Warrington.— Advt. BUItGLAItY AT RAINIIILL.

On Sunday night or early on Monday morning the house of Mr. Carthers, at Rainhill, was entered by burglars and ramsacked from top to bottom. The thieves had obtained access by forcing up the lower cash of the front parlour window, thus breaking the catch. It is doubtful whether they had entered while the family were at church on Sunday evening and secreted themselves or during the night while the family were asleep. On Mr. Carthers going downstairs on Monday morning he was surprised to find the floors littered with the contents of boxes drawers, workboxes, &c., but strange to say nothing was missing. He communicated with the police, who, on inspecting the house, said these men were after money only. Not being able to find any coin they had helped themselves to the contents of the pantry and a decanter of spirits. BASAIN t rrt s. Garland, Ironmonger, Warrington and Earleatown

EXPECTID STOPPAGB OF COCKHBDGB IA ILLS. The employees at the Cock hedge Mills of Messrs. -Armitage and Rigby, Limited, Warrington, leave off for their five days' Easter holidays on Thursday. On the same day a fortnight's notice was given to them that the mills were to be closed, no that they will only have a week's work on returning from their holidars, unless, as is possible, the notice is in the meantime withdrawn. This step has been taken by Messrs. Armitage and Rigby in accordance with the resolution of the Federation of Master Cotton Spinners, of which they are members, to close the mills consequent upon the Stalyoridge strike. It is the spinning department that is directly affected by this movement, but as the weaving department is dependent upon the spinners for their material the whole establishment of some 1,300 employees will thus be stopped. , lie other cotton mill in War- rington, the Florence Mill, not being affiliated with the Masters' Federation will not be affected. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. Durros, Sankey-et. Warrington.—Adrt.

div.head: GOOD FRIDAY AT WIDNRS AND RUNCORN.
div.p: GOOD FRIDAY AT WIDNRS AND RUNCORN.

As far as —practicable the various works in these towns were at a standstill yesterday. The usual Raster services were held at most of the churches and chapels, and in the-evening tea parties were held in several of the Nonconformist Schools. The weatber was fine but cold and the number of pleasure seekers was not very large. At Runcorn, railway traffic was stopped entirely, and at Midnes trains were run as on Sundays. When in want of a chaste and elegant wedding or birthday present go to PRITCEARD°B, 51, High-st.--Adtit. •

div.head: STEALING EGGS AT RAINHILL.
div.p: STEALING EGGS AT RAINHILL.

At Widnes l'etty-es-sio—n-s-, on Thursday, Geo. Oakes, Owens-road, Rainhill, was charged with stealing 15 eggs. value is., the property of Mr. Stapleton Bretherton, J.P., Rainhill. The prisoner was employed on the Home Farm and was warned by the bailiff not to go near a certain stack whet. a hen was sitting. Afterwards the eggs were missed and egg-shells were found in the prisoners pockets, and there were marks upon his clothing. The prisoner admitted the offence and was fined 10s. MAINTENANCE OF A WIFE AT RUNCORN.

liefore Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Thomas at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, Edward James Waterson, of Widnes, was charged with having failed to contri- bute towards his wiles maintenance under an order of the Court. The prisoner had not made a payment since the order was made on the 7th February, and there was 30s. in arrears, and costs 103. 61.—The prisoner who said he had been out of work and could not pay, and de- clined to make any offer, and he was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment. If you wantyour watch repaired by skilful workmen, take it to PRITCHAMYS.—Atet.

div.p: TIIII A LLINIRD BIGAMY AT RUNCORN.

Joseph Partington Ankers, aged 26 years, was again brought up at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of having feloniously married Anne Edwards his former wife, Priscilla, being then alive.— Supt. Atherton stated that he would be compelled to ask for a further adjournment of a week, as an important ivitness living at Brymbo, Denbighshire, had failed to attend.—lnspector Cooper produced the certificates of the two marriages, and the prisoner was remanded until Wednesday next. JOSILPH PRlTCHAND.Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High- at., and 4, Brldge-et., Runcorn.—Adrt. CONFIRMATION SRI:MICR 111. T RUNCORN.

On Wednesday evening the Bishop of Chester, Dr. Jayne, conducted a confirmation service at Runcorn Parish Church. in the presence of a crowded congrega- tion. The candidates numbered 115, and were presented from the following churches :—Parish. 35 males and 38 females ; Holy Trinity, 2 males and 3 fethales ; Weston Point, 3 males and 4.ferailei ; and Halo-, 9 males and 18 females. The clergy present were Rev. Canon M. Wood, Dr. Preston, G. D. Wray (Halton), T. H. Wilcockson (Weston Point), A. H. Riley, G. H. Seeley, C. S. Montgomery, and J. Holden. The Bishop delivered two interesti ig addresses, one before and the other after the laying on of hands. JOORPH PRITCHARD keeps spectacles to 8111 all sights from a shilling a palr.—Adrt. PRISENTATION TO A FORMER RUNCORN MINISTER.

A few days ago the Rev. J. D. Thomas, who resigned the pastorate of Bethesda Congregational Church. Run- corn, upwards of two years ago, was the recipient of a very handsome present. The rev. gentleman left this town to take charge of the Derby-at. Congregational Church, Bolton. over which he now presides. He has a united and prosperous church, and is performing a good work there ow the "forward movement" lines. The presentation took the form of a purse of gold, and was made in connection with the Pleasant Sunday Afternoon society, whose winter session has just closed. A hope was expressed that the money would enable Mr. Thomas to spend a pleasant holiday during the summer. It you want a lucky welding ring go 1051, lixon-sr.,where you will gets present with it.—Anet. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, under the presidency of Mr. U. Coleburn, and there were pre- sent Messrs. E. Imison Whittler.and W. F.Salkeld (sec.). The report showed that the interments for the year ended March 25th, numbered 525, compared with 491 for the corresponding period last year. The fees received during the same period amounted to £452 15s. 4d. ; pre- vious year, £449 es. 41. The minutes of the Finance Committee were approved, on the motion of Mr. Imi- son, and it was decided to complete a mortgage of £534 3s. at 31, which had been negotiated by the secretary. Arrangements made by time secretary for the better con- trol of the cemetery, so far as grave digging was con- cerned, were approved...
'SOSEP.II PRITCWARD has the best stock of ladies' silver awd gold watches In the town.—Advt. I WILL DISPUTED M A RUNCORN TRLDESMAN.

A the Manchester County Court, theother day, before his Honour Judge Heywood, an action was hoard in which George Frederick Croley and John Croley sought to establish the will of John Musgrave Croley late of Elizabeth Ann-st., Rochdale-road, Manchester. The validity of the will was disputed by the defendant, Wm. Croley, boot-maker, Runcorn.—Mr. Suttcn was coun- sel for the plaintiffs. and Mr. Wynne Humphreys ap- peared for the defendant. After hearing the evidence, his Honour asked Mr. Humphreys what course he in- tended to pursue, and Mr. Humphreys, after consulting his client, said he did not thinlk he was in a position to contest the will, wept by imputing deliberate perjury. He did not feel quite justified in making that charge against the witnesses, and therefore as far asl his client was concerned, he might say he did not propose to con- test-the will further.—His Honour then said he thought the course Mr. Humphreys bad taken was both a wise and proper -course. .He pronounced in favour of the will, and directed that each party should pay their own costs, the costs of the plaintiffs, howevet to come out of the estate.

Peter Knight, was summoned to appear before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, to answer a charge of deserting his wife and family.—The defendant failed to appear.—Mr. E. W. Humphreys, for the complainant, stated that the parties were married in September, 187 e, and there were five children of the union, the oldest being .15 rears and the youngest 16 months. They had never lived happily together, hut so long as the com- plainant's mother lived and kept the family in tolerable comfort and the sum of £3OO the mother left the com- plainant lasted, Knight seemed to have thought he could get on,pretty well, but when that money was expended lie commenced to lit use his wife, as was evidenced by the fact that he had been convicted no fewer than six times for assaults upon Irr, and that on two occasions separation orders had been made by the Bench. The last order was broken through force, the woman being un- able to prevent h,in coming into the house and she not' understanding quite her legal position allowed the mat- ' ter to remain there. The complainant had not lived with the defendant for 13 weeks. He had left the town, land had been tiavelling in theisle of Man ands Dublin, I and had been spending money recklessly. The defend- ant deliberately declined to do anything forcthe support of hie wife and family and she could not get any money from him. le could earn 30s. a week if he would and Mr. Hutnphreys asked the magistrates to make such an order, as would prevent the woman and her children from going to the Workhouse.—Annie Knight, of Z King-st., -t-.oe wife of the defendant, corroborated this statement and said his mother kept the defendant. —The Bench made a maintenance order of .1.55. per week upon the defendant. who was also ordered to pay the costs of 21s. , .10SOPli Perronantt, Watchmaker and Jeweller. la. After a very brief illness Mr. Isaac Stubbs, of Lynwood Rouse, Normin-roed. Runcorn, died on Tuesday morning. Hs caught a chill on the previous Wednesday, which settled into inflatneaation of the lunge, and despite the medical skill ef•Drs. Robin- 'son and McKenzie, in consulta•ion with Br. Glynn, of LieerpooL•he succumbed as stated. 21orn.nt Bates Bridge, Runcorn, in 1851, he was while yet a baby in arms taken by his parents to Darwen, in Lanca- shire. where le remained for about 30 years. For a number of years he was• employed in a cottizin will, but subsequently he obtained a more congenial position under Mr, Barnes, mineral water manufac- turer, and having obtained a knowledge of the secrets of the trade, he returned to his native place in 2880 and set op in business on his own account. Hemet with marked success, and his business extended by leaps and bounds. He established works at Runcorn and North-. wich Atted up with machinery of the most modern and, ;effective type, necessary to carry out the demands made I by his widely extended custom, Be occupied at the. Ittmeof his death.the honourable position of Ilice-presi.' dent of the Liverpool and District Mineral Water Manufacturers' Association, and the snembers con- templated raising him to the position of President. li' religion Mr. Stubbs was a Baptist, but there being no church where he could worship according to the tenets of his faith, heeded himself to the Methodist Free‘Church, in the concerns of which he took an active and useful part, and was held in high esteem. In politics he was a Liberal, and although he did not ac ively promulgate his views, he held fisinly t. his principles, and, he was respected'by those who held opposite views. He was a member of the Order of Free, masons and was associated with the Ellesmere Lodge, Runcorta. Genial, charitable, and upright in character he had hosts of 'friends and was a highly respected member of the community in wtuch he lived. He had only attained 42 years of age, and leaves a widow and live children to mourn his loss. div.head: INCORPORATION OF WIDNES. THE SCHEME PUBLISHED.
div.p: THE INCORPORATION OF WIDNES. THE SCHEME PUBLISHED.

The charter which is to convert the Local Board district of Widnes into a corporate borough, is now within measurable distance of receiving the Royal assent and signature. Last week end the scheme of incorporation as amended by the London Author- ities,. was published in " The Gazette," and for a month opportunity will be afforded for any person interested to raise objections. At the expiration of that time, should there be no opposition, and there is not the slighteit prooability of any, the scheme will be submitted to the Privy Council for their approval, and seal, and the signature of Ller Majesty will be affixed, and the long expected charter will be forwarded to Widnes.

The scheme sets forth that it shall come into operation 11 on the day of the first meeting of the Council of the Municipal borough created by the charter, or at the date of its confirmation by Parliament or Order in , Council,whichever is later. Immediately from and after the commencement of the scheme, the Local Board should be abolished, together with all its jurisdiction, powers, and authority whatsoever,and the Mayor,alder- men, and burgesses and their officers being substituted for the Local Board and their offers. The School Board for the township should continue to be the School Board for the municipal borough of Widnes, and all charges charged on the poor rate and school fUnd of the town- ship, immediately before the commencement of this scheme, should be charged upon the borough rate or fund and th school fund of the School Board for the borough of Widnes respectively, and not otherwise, All the powers, rights, duties, capacities, liabilities, obligations, and property exercisable by, attaching to,or vested in the Local Board under the Local Acts and Orders shall pass to and be exercisable by, attached to, and vest in the Mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough, acting by the Council as the Sanitary Autho- rity of the borough. The power of appointing two governors of the foundation known as the Farnworth Grammar School, conferred upon the Local Board by the Charity Commissioners should rest in and be exercisable by the Borough Council. Provision is made for auditing the accounts of the Local board. The concluding clause of the scheme provides that in case any officer of the Local Board who shall have been employed by them for a period of at least five years shall not be employed by the Council of the said borough, nor offered by the said Council a position in their employ of a similar character and of an equal value to that formerly held by him, he shall be entitled to be paid by way of compensation for the loss of his position out of the funds of or under the control of the Mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough such annual allowance or such gratuity as on a full consideration of the circumstances of the ease may seem to the Lords Commissioners of her Majesty's Treasury to be a reasonable and just compensation for the loss of his position ; and the said Commissioners, in awarding the said compensation, shall be guided by the principles which would be applicable in the case of an award of compensation under the provisions of the Superannua- tion Act, 1859, to a person retiring or removed from the public service in consequence of the abolition of his office, provided that no special minute within the mean- ing of the said Act stating any special grounds for granting such allowance shall be necessary or be made, and provided, nevertheless, that if any such officer be so employed by the said Council, end discharged by theta for any other cause I than inefficiency, breach of duty, or misconduct within two years after the commencement of this scheme, he shall be entitled to compensation in the same manner as if he had not been employed by the said Council ; pro- vided also that the term " officer" shall include only all salaried persons employed by the said Local Board whose salaries or emoluments are payable at intervals of not less tban a month ; provided also Oat the said Com- missioners shall be the sole judges as to the right or clairmpf any officer to any compensation whatever, and as to the amount thereof, arid upon any question what- ever which may arise under this clause, and the deter- mination of the Land Commissioners shall be exclueive and final.

TION. SPEECH BY MIL. WAD-DEACON.

Under the auspices of this association, a public., meeting was held in the Baths Assembly Room, on Monday evening, and there was a very large atten- dance of both sexes. Mrs. O'Keeffe occupied the chair,and she was supported by the members of the committee and by Dr. o•Keeffe, Mr. F. Hartland,and Mr. .11. Wade-Deacon, J.P., C.C. Mrs. Stewart Brown (daughterof Mr. E. K. Muspratt) wrote regretting ber inability to be present. owing LO a prior engagement. Referring to a recant visit to Ireland, she said the sad condition of theveople contrasted pain- fully with the beautiful acenery.and they could only hope, ,that the time was not far distant when the Irish should smile as nature did in their country. They could al,l do something towards hastening forward that happy time by working for the return of Mr. Gladstone to power,a.nd she was sure the Liberal women of Widnes would not be behind their sisters in other parts of the country in help- ing to secure that result. (Applause.) , Mrs. O'Keeffe then delivered a brief speech, in which she congratulated the members on the success of the asso- ciation. She had no idea that the wOmen of Widnes were ench

div.head: INTHCISILSTIC 1001.1TICIANS.
div.p: INTHCISILSTIC 1001.1TICIANS.

And she ho?ed that the association would continue to grow until its members could he counted not by hun- dreds but by thousands. (Applause.) The result of the -recent County Council election was very satisfactory to them, and she had been told that the women of the as- sociation had materially assisted in that election. (Hear, ,hear.) She hoped they would give the same assistance In securing the return of their .candidate to Parliament. .(Applause.) Mr. Deacon' who was enthusiastically greeted, re: ••; the Women's Alisociation had sprung into life at • •,e .bound, and it had already ,done considerable 'work. (applause.) He was much indebted to the women for the work they had done for him at the recent County Council election, and also tomany members of party,who worked so zealously and so successfully for him whilst he was laid up. That election had demonstrated that the Liberals could have the candidate of their choice in-South Widnes, and the victory gained had inspired him with stronger hopes than he had before of success at the General Election. (Applause.) But they must not rely too much on the recent contest, for they had .a hard tlght before them. Widnes waS the Liberal stronghold, and it was by winning . votes in Widnes that they could counterbalance the votes outside. The people must be persuaded and who could persuade them like the Widnes ladie.s? (Laughter.) On a future occasion he would deal with the speeches delivened at the Conservative meeting in the Drill Hall, but there was one thing he could not refrain from noticing. • certain gentleman said that as he (Mr. Deacon) was no lonvor engaged in the chemical works he would soon be leaving the town like the rest of them. If there was any reason why he should leave Widnes, he ,could have dime so before, because his business did not necessitate him liv- ing in Widnes. The other gentlemeet.eould manage their business by living away, and he migbt have done the same had he wished. (Applause.) A stranger perhaps would not care to come and settle down in Widnes ; but he was not a stranger.. ,His home had always been in Widaes,and he felt the force of the old song that " There is no place likehorne." (Applause.) He had no interest' elsewhere like he had in Widnes, and the ladies of his family weee willing to throw in their lot with him. He did not wish to be idle, and he had no desire to leave while he could work for the town. (Applause.) It was an extraordinary commentary upon the attack upon him that a special tram was engaged to carry all the Tory speakers to their homes. (Laughter, and applause.) Alluding to Irish affairs, Mr. Deacon said the Local , Government Bill would not settle the matter any more I than the land question, and their opponents were afraid of bringing the bill forward fora second reading. Nothing would remedy the state of the country but the passing of a Home Rule Bill. (Applause.) . . . _

TIM A LERGED SYSTEMATIC Flllt/DS.-Orl Tuesday, at Frodsham Police Court, before Messrs. C. Reynolds and A. Thomas, a man named James Turner, of Newtown, Frodsham, was charged, on remand, with fraudulently collecting alms from different farmers and tradesmen in the neighbourhood. Several witnesses spoke to giving the prisoner money on the representation that he required it to bury two of his children. It. was shown that no deaths had taken place in his family.—Committed to goal for 14 dayg. GUARDIA% Eircnoxs.—Great interest has been mani- fested in the Guardians for Frodsham, which was the anly township where there was a contest. The voting papers were counted at Dutton Workhouse, on Monday, under the superintendence of Mr. J. Ashton, clerk to the Union, who was returning officer. The result is as follows E. Heywood, 326 J. M. Williams, 174 ; H. G. Linaker, 153; anti J. Edwards, 112. The two hrst named gentlemen were declared elect ed,and it will be ob- served that Mr. Williams takes the place previously held I by Mr. Edwards. • filiture of the contest is the large number of voter recorded for Mr. Heywood in compari- son with the other candidates. OPENING OF A TEMPERANCE CAFE. On Saturday afternoon a caf4 at Frodsham Bridge was formerly opened by Mrs. Tornkinson. of Willington Hall, wife of Mr. James Tomkinson, Liberal candidate for the Eddisbury Division. During the past six months a social club has been carried on with considerable in- terest in connection with the Union Church. The ladies of the congregation entered Into the undertaking with • spirit and deterrnination,and each evening some of them were present to attend to the wants of the members. The club has thus proved a couuter-attraction to the , public-house, and has been the means of promoting I temperance in the locality. The officials are—Presidenr I the Rev. Charles Craddock; secretary, Mr. Th6mae Turner: treasurer, Mr. E. G. Aitken • committee. Messrs. T. A. Rigby, John Pemberton, Samuel Helsby, Joseph Hinde, W. J. Owen, Harry Turton, and Robert Booth. The membership is about 60. In order to de- velop the work, premises close to Frodsham Bridge have been placed at the disposal of the club by Mr. Rigby. These have been fitted up with all the auxiliaries for the convenience and pleasure of the members, and, in ad- dition, visitors to Frodsham can have the privilege of having refreshments. The place will be conducted on temperance principles. Belonging to it will be a bowl- ing green and several rowing boats on the river. Tea was provided in Union Church at five o'clock, and afterwards an adjournment was made to the Cafe, which Mrs. Tomkinson then declared open. She said if they were to succeed in the temperance reformation, it must be by reducing the numerous temptations in the way of the people, and this could best be dono by pro-

viding counter-attractions where the people could go and rationally enjoy themselves without partaking of intoxi— cating drinks. Subsequently a meeting was held in the Union Church, under the presidency of the Rev. C. , Craddock, who was supported by Mr. ad Mrs. Tomkin- , seri, the Rev. P. Pisey, the Rev. Mr. Edmonds. Mr. T. Rigby, C.Ald.. Mr. Fari,h, J.P., (Heisby). Mr. Edward Jackson, Mr. Rhodes, Mr. Beck, and Mr. Arthur Rigby. Addresses were delivered by the Chairman. Mr. A. Rigby, Mrs. Timlinson, and Mr. Tomlinson. Votes of thank*. concluded the proceedings.

Foornam. Marca.—The fixture Lymm Grammar School v. Penketh Friends' School was played on the ground of the former on Saturday. From the kick-off the Lymm youths pressed very hard. When time was called the score stood : Grammar School, 13 goals; Penketh Friends' School, one goal. MS LOCAL BOARD.—It id stated that Mr. Rogers, who has for many years been a member of the Local Board, has sent in his resignation to the clerk, to be placed before the Board at the next meeting. The resignation of Mr. Rogers will be received with ri gret by all sections of the communits , and it is stated that an effort will be made to induce him to re-consider the position which he has taken up. WIT3LEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVISMINT SOCIETY—The COD- eluding meeting of the session was held on Monday even- ing. There was a very good attendance. The business was only of a formal character, and consisted in the election of officers as follows: Mr. Brown and Mr. Thorp, presidents; Mr. G. Brereton, treasurer ; Mr. Rogerson. secretary; committee: Mr. E. Moaton, Mr. J. Upson, Mr. G. Allen. A supper was afterwards pro- vided, the catering being entrusted to the Misses Machin. TEN WHIT-WIOOL Gm...4..—A meeting of the representa- tives of the various B4nds of Hope in the district was held on Saturday evening. The business was to discuss the form of the demonstration, and the attendant items. Mr. Dodds presided. There was not a large attendance, and as the meeting was not of a thoroughly representa- tive character, ne serious business was transacted. It was intimated that Mrs. Grundy had decided not to allow the use of her fields for the assembly ira. future.

CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF HOPE.—The last entertain- ment of the session was held on Monday evening. The Rev. Charles Clay, 8.A., presided. There was a very good audience. The proaramme consisted of the well. known children's cantata "rue bundle of sticas," or " Santa Claus." The characters wore very well sus- tained as follows : —Santa Claus, A Ast ley ; Aunt Rachel, Clara Daniels ; Mabel, M. Drinkwater ; Dot, F. Brierley ; Dick,J. R. Barton. Very good effects were produced by the choruses. One chorus by 20 small children was ex- . . . _ .

„ , ceptionally well rendered. A choir of 40 voices assisted. , Prizes were awarded during the evening to the reciters who had taken part in the meetings during the winter. special feature of the presentation was the award of I' dulls to the smaller children. ADDREAS ON GEOLOGY AND THE CREATION OF TEE WOULD.—Mr. Thomas Morris, F.U.S., of Warrington. 1 delivered an address in the Congregational Chapel, ' Lvmm, on t!:unday afternoon, upon thc words: "And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness,” &c. He contended, in an interesting address on the creation of the world, that the chapter from whichi the words were taken gave the most concise his- tory of the formation of the earth which hid ever been penned. The order taf the six days' work was most excellent—the first day found the earth without form and void; the sixth day found it fit for the recep- tion of man. The young on reading the words, "Arid the evening and the morning were the first day," would come to the conclusion that only 24 hours elapsed between etch of the working days, and they would, therefore be startled by the mention of any- thing approaching a contradiction to that by him. Like every science connected with natural history, geo- logy might be made a source of pleasure and true enjoy- ment at a very small expense of time or trouble, though the links by which it was connected with other sciences ma- tbe perceived and understood. They say that be- tween the evenings and mornings of the third, fourth, and fifth days, myriads of years had rolled by, that their earth had made its thousand times ten thousand revolu- tions round the sun, and had resolved or turned round on its own axis 380 times tor each revolution it made round the sun, was not saying a word which was con- trary to the spirit in which Moses wrote. During the evening Mrs. Pearson, of Warrington, sang two sacred solos, and Messrs. Pearson and Payton contributed twe duets (violin and organs.)

div.p: WA RRINGTON CRICKET AND BOWLING

CLUB. How cheering is the brighter lengthened day When winter's frosty winds have passed away, The ice-bound earth by gentle gales set free, And birds sing loud upon the budding tree. While death's long shadows dark with human woe, Diminish when the sunny south winds blow. Then fields with early flowers are gaily clad. And all things seem so beautiful and glad. With welcome spring. our friends once more to greet, Rejoiced again in healthy sport to meet. ITo view the charming sod renewed in grAisa, Where many a well-contested game has been. In leisure hours the scenes are kept alive, While tennis bowls and manly cricket thrive Where freedom lives and discord is not sowh, And no disturbing politics are known. With differing thoughts true friendship here may shine, A ray of beauty and all )wer divine, Above the weeds of selfishness and strife That only mar the happiness of life. No low ambition's vain deceitful show, Whose selfish heart no Bympath7 may know. Allures from peace with all her pompous pride, Or leads us from dear simple nature wide. But summer breathes 1113011 the flowers that play To zephyrs dancing with declining day ; Delighted here from anxious cares we rest Till twilight deepens in the purple west. Warrington, April 11, 1892.

Secretaries of Football Cluba are requested to note that reporta of matchee played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.

RUGBY. Faonsaus•. STOCKPORT " A."—This match was played at Stockport, on Saturday, in grand weather. At half- time the score Stood,Stockport "A," one goal (dropped) ; Frodsham, nil. In the second half Frodsham had all the best of the play, penning the home team in their own 25 the whole time, but through sheer ill-luck they were unable to score. Final score—Stockport, four points ; Frodsham, nil. WARRINGTON A v. Tra.nEstaint A. At Warrington. The contest was started by the home team, Hampson, by a capital bit of work, forcing the game into the visitors' quarters. A free kick to Tyldesley removed the threatened danger, but Potts, with a dashing run, carried hostilities close to the line. The defenders cleared splendidly; and a lot of mulling by the home team found the ball dribbled over the line and touched down. Fine play between Warburton, Knowles, and Molyneux soon found the combatants vieing with one another on the centre line, where Hampson made a fine dribble. This invasion was quickly repulsed by the Tyldesley team, but Lawless was the means of relief, Lally, Nevvey, Higham, and Molyneux subsequently taking the struggle to neutral territory, where an excellent piece of passing between Newsy, Forster, Knowles, and Lawless, ended in the latter getting a capital try. A minute later, Warburton, Samp- son, and Forster were prominent in the ball being I rushed over, the last-named scoring. Then Daniels and Knowles put in a neat piece of play, but Smith kicked to touch at midfield. Potts and LaWless soon had , the ball back, and some passing by Barnes and Lally saw Potts rush over. Tyldeslef had now shot their bolt, and after Smith had saved a rush, Barnes ran clean round, and passed to Daniels, who scored. Sampson then ran strongly for Barnes to get a try, and at half- time, Warrington led by five tries. Re-starting the game, the hotne team quickly forced four minors, and after Warburtoa had kicked to the line, Barnes threw to Daniels, who dodged over. The drop-out found Tyldes- ley reaching midfield, but the home forwards screwed the pack grandly, rushing the leather to the goal, and after it had been splendidly passed from hand to hand, Potts obtained possession, and dashed across the line in fine style. The same player kicked a goal. Another minor followed,an I some sensational play was witnessed, Barnes being the chief operator, by a grand dodgy run. Sampson, by strong forward play, was very noticeable, more minors ensuing, and then Warburton scored, quickly followed by Potts, who kicked a goal frcin his try. The Tyldesley men were utterly overplayed, bei lc/ completely able to cope with the fine all round play of their opponents, try after try being obtained, Danie a, W. Warburton, Forster, Barnes. and J. Warburto t, scoring, the full total amounting to four goals, ten tries, seven miners to one minor. RUNCORN v. STOCKPORT.

These Cheshire organizations met at Runcorn on Sat- urday, when the home team asserted their supremacy to the tune of four tries, or eight points, to nil. This result is all the more surprising considering that Run- corn were minus such excellent players as Crompton, Massey, Pendlebury, and Robinson, and speaks volumes for the able display given by the suestitutes. Poets started the oval, and after a spell of monotonous scrim- mages, the combination of Runcorn asserted itself, and Davies running through the thick of his opponents, wound up a brilliant piece of play by passing to May for the latter to score under the posts. The same player failed at the somewhat easy place. Even play marked the proceedings until near the interval, when Abrams, May, and Davies passing well, a second try was manipu- lated, but still no goal accrued. With four pints to the good, the second half was restarted, but the persistent off-side tactics adopted by Noble, whose mission appar- ently was to play wing forward, spoiled what would otherwise have been an interesting game. Severe corn ments were made on, the style adopted by the ex-Brad- ford man, but dispite this player's wrongful tactics, Runcorn again broke through the Stockport defence, and at the close the homesters were in a majority by four tries to nil. WIDNES v. WALKDEN. _

The return match between the above teams was played on Saturday, on the Widnes ground. The visitors kicked off, arid rushed up in touch. Farmer picked up, and after some splendid forward passing, the leather was rushed up near the home line, but was returned to three- quarters, but Was once more in the home quarters but was eventua ly kicked dead. Immediately alter the kick- out Johnson made a brave attempt to score, but just failed. The oval was then rushed down the field by the visitors, an an unsuccessful aitempt made at goal. Play was new centred in mi.:-field. Peters at this point was making his " mark," when one of the vi,itors rushed up and charged foully. This naturally enraged the Whi- nesians, but happily, the referee interposed before any further scene was witnessed. A few minutes after play was resumed. Drummond rushed well up arid placed the hall over, but Barber failed to improve. At kick-out, the hall was returned in touch near the goal . line. At half-time the seore was—Widnes, one try ; Walkden, nil. On play being resumed, the visitors ran up the field, a scrimmage ensuing, from which the ball , wis picked our, and an attempt- at goal proved success- ful. A short time after. the leather was again dribbled up to the visitors' line and made things appear danger- ous, but Cross nicely saved. The play now became most exciting, and the home team hail the advantage of their opponents, when by a " fluky " chance the ball was picked up again and dropped over the visitors' cross- bar. Scarcely five minutes remained for the Widres boys to endeavour to improve their score, and they played very pluckily and were gaining ground nicely, butt were I brought back two or three times by the referee. They did not lose heart, but followed the leather well up, and when within a yard of the line another scene took place between the players, and it is alleged that one of the visitors struck Wright whilst on the ground. The spec- tators came rushing overtime ground, arid the game was declared to be finished ; but the crowd was so enraged that protection had to be obtained to escort the offe.4A- ing player to the Waggonette. Finsl result :—Walkdbn, 8 points ; Widnes, 2.

div.head: RUNCORN v. WARRINGTON.
div.p: RUNCORN v. WARRINGTON.

A re-union between these teams having taken place, a l friendly match was Oki ed on the Irwell-lane enclosure, Runcorn, on Wednesday evening. It will be remembered bx the followers of the game, that some four years ago the two teams engaged in a fight for the West Lanca-.. shire Cup, when Warrington proved victorious in the replayed tie at Southport. There thon took place what was considered some rough play, r hich aroused such a vast amount of ill-feeling that a rupture ensued between the two combinations, the result being that no fixtures could be arranged for them be engage in friendly rivalry. It is pleasing to find that at last a reconciliation has taken place, and this has been hailed with satisfaction by the partisans of both teams; and an earnest hope Is entertained that nothing will come to cause them to be at loggerheads or at variance one with another. The weather was of a most inclement description, snow falling heavily for half-an-hour before the com- mencement ot hostilities, and there being a storm during part of the time the match -proceeded. Not- withstanding this climatic drawback, there was large crowd lining tire enclosure. The enthusiasiic . reception osf the players, as they stepped on the ttfrf, was a proof of the pleasure experienced by the specta- tors, arid that they were ready and willing to again engage in friendly combat. It was somewhat unfortu- nate that both sides were short of usual first team players. It was fully half an hour after tie advertised time before operations were commenced, a circumstance to a great extent due to the awful atmospheric condi- tions which prevailed. Tire teams faced each ot her AA follows :—Runcorn, S. Houghton, back ; Faulkner, Davies, and Hotting worth, three-quarter backs ; A bra ms and Li Robinson, half-backs ;0. Hughes, W. stiaw, J. Gayter, H. Williams, G. Lee, J. Davies, A. Taylor, P. Riley, and M. Darb,% shire, forwards. Warriagton i—J. Bussow, hack ; Wm.-quarter backs, J. W. Evans, F. Heesom, and C. Potts ; half-hacks, J. T. Ilite arid James Bate; forwards' D. Ashton, T. Donohue, Fair. Turner, W. Handles, E. Bailey, Teare, J. Holum's, W. Dines, and A.Newry. P. Riley kicked oil, to which" Smack ' Bate replied. Ad er the usual preliminaries play was found at centre, Fair. Turner came grandly through the ' pack, but threw forward with a reckless pass. Abrams relieved, and kicked well up the field, to which Ihtssow replied, turd Houghton dallying trio long with the ball, play located dangerously near the home line. /MAY allfi Gayter got Die sphere away. and Fritts was coilare.l before he could put in anything like an effective reply. Some tall kicking .13etween the respeCtiv'e full backs ended in the internsi tonal putting Die ball in touch near the centre flag. served the loud applause which was given by the specta- tors, it being of a really superb character. The restart ' found Warrington invading the home quarters, until Owen Hughes, with a brilliant dribble, forced the visi- tors back, Turner saving at the right moment. Half- time was shortly afterwards called, with Runcorn one goal, to Warrington one minor. Turner re- commenced, to which Houghton responded, and Ashton, getting possession, tried to break through. Abrams, however, was sufficient for the occa- sion, and he removed the danger. The warfare was then once again carried on in the visitors' territory. Passing between Bate and Evans saw the latter player making a movement on the right. The game was now fought with great determination, the ball rapidly travelling from end to end. A bout of brilliant passing between the two Bates again caused an attack on the home lines, but Faulkner sent them to the right- about. The game then became rough, and Heesom and H. Williams getting at variance, the referee was called upon to caution them. This was a scene much to be regretted, especially seeing that the match was of a reconciliatory character. Abrams next essayed to break away, but Heesom frustrated his efforts, although a moment later Davies made a good attempt, and Boscow -being at fault, Evans was just in time to save. J. T. Bate, however, succeeded in averting danger, and some bad passing by the home backs let in the visitors, Flollingworth mulling several good chances. Robin- son next got off with a good run along touch, which again placed the citadel of Warrington in jeopardy. The visiting forwards again removed the threatened danger, and a free kick enabled them to gain further ground. Houghton was now prominent with some tricky play, his kicking at this stage being very serviceable. Peter Riley, with a grand dribble, again got into close quar- ters, Boscow being held before he could reply. Time was called with the ball on the visitors' lines. Runcorn won a severely contested game by one goal to Warring- ton one minor or five points to nothing. • WARRINGTON v. TYLDESLEY.

Fine summerlike weather favoured this return match, at Tyldesley, on Saturday, and a " gate," numbering nearly four thousand, witnessed the game. Warrington were booked favourites during the week, their substan- tial victory in the first engagement, no doubt, account' lag for this. However, those who had pinned their faith to the chances of the visitors were not quite so sanguine when it was seen that Nevins, Donohue+, Berry, and Thorniley were absentees—a quartette of forwards who are just suited for the heavy" Bongers."

It was a little after four o'clock- when Turner kicked off, against a strong breeze, and what proved to be a sensational thirty-five minutes. For Webster being obstructed in responuing to a kick by Evans, a kick into touch landed the oval at Tyldesley quarters, but some huge punting by Shaw arid Berry took play direct to the Warrington lines. Jolley, Bandies, and westall were prominent in a slight relief to the half.way flag, but Shaw had a shot at goal, and a minor was recorded. Tyldesley still attacked, and Boscow and none of the three-quarters could make any headway in the least. The Tyldesley forwards were very energetic, and ,rush in g finely, Evans helped up a sequence of passes by a capital run to the visitors' lines. An appeal for a try went against the Tyldesley men, but from a scrimm- age the home forwards rushed the Warring- ! tonians over, and Fell scored, a point whick Straw improved upon. Turner restarted, but no ; impression could be made on the Tylasley lines, and a run by J. Fearnley was responded to be B'iscow. Flee- sore, Bate, and Antrobus tried their hands at the passing game, but to no purpose; the tackling was accurate, ! Bate, indeed, having a rival in Hansom, whose mission seemed to be to watch the county man. A grand kick by Boscow realized hail way, and Berry tried to get away, but on this occasion met his match in Ashton. The International, a moment later, screwed finely to touch, and Warrington were again having an anxious time of it. From a scrimmage near the line Hansom dodged over, and Shaw again did the needful. With ten points in arrears, the game was resumed, and although Jolley and Evans put in some fine play, the Warringtonians tailed to pass the quarter flag. Still the game was a trifle more even, and Bata and Antrobus, with several passes, even- tually handed the oval to Webster, for the latter to punt to Taylor, and the response again found Warrington defending. Tyldesley were obstinate, and attack they did in earnest, for, despite a short dribble by Ashton, an over-anxiety neutralized the slight advantage, an the oval was kept continually careering about the Warring- ton quarters. A dribble by Turner realized a relief of ten yards, but Fearnley responded in true style, and Boscow was lucky in saving a rush headed by Woodward and Shepherd. Evans arid Fleesom next saved well, whilst a neat display by Bate and Antrobus sent: up the hopes of the Warrington a linirers a goodly percentage. Webster grassed Taylor finely on one occasion, when scoring seemed a certainty, but from a scrimmage which was immediately formed, Hansom passed to Berry, and the latter got in near the posts, Shaw again doing the needful. Taylor and Shaw wer., responsible for the leaders maintaining the attack, and although Hansom found touch near the line, Bate, Tur- ner, and Jolley came ;iveav from the ruck, and play was now of a give-and-take nature at neutral ground. Once Tyldesley got aeay to the line, and Berry got in again, , but a pass forward overruled the point. Antrobus was held in dangerous proximity to the posts, and from a kick by the same player Fearnley made Iris mark, Shaw trying at goal, but this trifle the second minor of the match was recorded. Boscow saved well near the close of this half, and after Randles had dribbled to half-way, the interval was called with the score—Tyldesley, 3-0-2 ; Warrington nil. It was a big lead the homesters had established, and one that would have disheartened many teams, arid Warrington went into the fray during the second half with nothing like their proper dash. Webster failed to respond to the kick riff, and it was left to Antrobus and late to place the Tyldesley men on the defensi vs. Berry was the saviour of his side from repeated disaster,. and hsffllng Antrobus on one occasion printed to Boscow, the litter's kick not being one of his best. Jolley, Ashton, : and Bate with individual efforts reached the home quar- ters, but Shaw, tackling Boscow with smart following up again relieved. The Warrington hack now registered the first minor for his side from beyond half-way, whilst in quick succession Turner and Heesom landed similar points. Buckley tackled Fearnley smartly on the line, bet again relief was forthcoming by Berry and Shaw. Jolley and Teare rushed the oval back again, whilst a combined rush of the whole nine Warrington for- wards ended in another minor, this last effort being indeed hard lines. Warrington now played with better combination, but scrimmages and line-outs monopolized the attention. Pretty passing by the Warrington half hacks was applauded to the echo, and near the close Bate ran finely, hut unluckily knocked on when opposition had been cleared. Antrohus, how- ever, punted to Ber7y, whose reply. was chargel. and Bate taking up the running, threw to Westhall (the latter having changed positions with Evans at three- quarter), and taking the pass cleverly, ran in a capital try, Turner placing a neat goal. Final result :Tyldesley, 3-0--2; Warring,to,n, 1-0-7. Tea ms —Warri ngton J. Boscow, back ;J. W. Evans, F. flopsen). and H. Webster, three-quarterbacks ;Ja-nes Bates and W. Antrohna, half hacks; H. Ashton, Fair. Turner, J. Jolley, W. Bandies, J. Teare, T. Donohue, Bailey, Westhall, Buckley, and J. Holmes, forwards. Tyldesley: P. Fearriley, back; Shaw, J. Fearnley, Evans, and Taylor, three-quarter hacks; Berry andllansom, half b icks ; Woodward, Sutcliffe, Fell, Shepherd; Worth- ington, Smith, Tinker, and Roberts, forwards.

We bear sometimes of eleven players of the same name contesting a game in cricket, but it is seldom that four brothers represent their club as backs in a football match, as was the case with• Hunslet versus Brighouse Rangers on Saturday. Walter Goldthorpe was full back, and his three brothers had the three-quarter play entrusted to them. Perhaps this comoination is the most powerful in the county.

. With regard to the subject of football running in families, I recollect two or three similar cases to that of the Goldthorpes in connection with Lancashire football. Four brothers Hunt played for Manchester and Preston, four Farrs for Swinton, and three Sawyers for Brough- ton. Three of the Hunts, I may add, played for Brig- land v. Scotland.

A large leather-covered basket which had been Tying unclaimed at the Barnsdale Rail Way Station. in North Gippsland, since the 6th of January last, has been for warded to the Melbourne police by the stationmaster, who had been led by the recent disclosures to suspect that it might prove in have sorae connection with ther Windsor murder. rif was addressed to Mrs' L. Dobs,andi upori the label being serapared with the prisoner's Deem- ' ing's, hand-writing, ir was at on apparent that the sus- picions of the railway officials were well founded. The basket was locked,' but by means of one of a bunch of keys found on Deeming when. he was arrested In I Western Australia, it was opened without the slightest I difficulty. It was found to contain's considepaile quan- tity of female apparel, including 801 rte linen bearing the .mark employed at Bueller's laundry..wfiither, it has been proved, " Drouin," as Deeming at thattirne called him- self, sent various bundles of clothing from No. 57, Andrew-street (where the murder was-committed), about the end of December. Inside the liming of the basket were portions of the "Liverpool Evening Empress" of the 29th of August, 1891. The signcance of this dis- covery lies in the fact that another portion of the same newspaper bearing the sawn date, was found upon the scene of the murder.

The dresses which the besket contained having been shown to Mr. Hirschfeldt, he immudiatelY identified them as having been worn by Mrs. Williams in board the KaiserWilhelna 11. during the outward voyage. In con- sequence of these fresh discoveries, which tend to show that precisely similar methods were'employed irt England and Australia tie get rid of the murdered woman's cloth- ing thevolice are causing a search to be made at every railway station, in the country, in the hope ofitrating the portions of the prisoner's luggage and effectS.which are it minting. . .

Deetning has, been very „quiet. He spends rno.it a his time in writing. When nolso engaged, he walks up and down his cellAncl discusses his case with his gablers. He speaks of the recent inquest as a "grand farce,"and says he is sorry it is at an end, as he is now deprived of all sources of amusement. To the governor of' the goal, speaking of the victim of the Windsor murder,.lie said, "She is not dead ;she will appear again all right." He continues to ask, for spirits and cigars,but is not allowed to have either He said to, the doctor on Saturday—re- ferring to the.brandy which was given him after the in- quest—" Why did yi,u give me that poison ,?":" Is is evident that he is doing his best to keep up the pretence of insanity,' As hezontinued to clamour for the spec- tacles whichtwere taken from him after his arrival,. the prison authorities have had his sight tested by oculists, and these gentlemenpronounce it perfectly good: The spectacles therefore-are still withheld from him: The Government medical officer, who has also exa- mined the prisoner,, believes him to be perfectlYsane. He was unable tb findianything that tended in thedeast to support the opposite•conclusion. Deeming,he,thinks„ is merely acting a part,, and is not even ding it skil- fully, being evidently a man with a certain, amount of superficial clevernessi, but no real deoth of character. The idea that the prisoner is not.entirely responsiMe for his actions is generally scouted, and no one would be greatly surprised if he.were to make a full confession. • A DOCTOR'S ESTIMATE OF DEEMING.

Leoutols, Aram:LE—lt is expected that the trial ef Deeming alias Williams will ccminence here on theth, Inst. It is not considered probable that the application of the defence loran adjournment, in order to permit of, witnesses being brought from England, will be granted Deeming has • been very orderly and industrious to-day. Be is still occupied in replying to the written inquiries of his solicito. The doctor, whom' Air. Lyle engaged in connection with the defence' has withdrawn front the case. He states that he has not taken this - eel:), owing to any lack of evi- dence, but in consequence of, what he considers the impossibility of. obtaining a fair hearing ins com- munity which is already prejudiced against the 'accused. He declares that Deeming belongs to the order of instinc- tive criminals, arid is as much wanting in the moral sense as a blind- man in the sense of sight, since killing is as much a part of his nature as eating. Ells head measure- ment is et,which is exceedingly small in comparison with his height. Deeming's whole character is one of extreme stupidity, and thejokes he makes are coarse and point- less. Ris escape hitherto, the doctor considers, has been due less to cunning than to accident.

div.p: The championship is not yet won, although it is long odds on Sunderland, who have to play the Rovers ati home and Darwin and Burnley away. It is quite pos- sible for them to lose the two latter, but if they win one they will will still count 38 points. North End have to meet Darwen and Accrington at home, and they should win both these, but they will have some difficulty in beating Aston Villa at Perry Bar. Should they succeed in winning all the three games they would reach 39 pointa.

- It is Wonderful how inch a powerful team as that of Everton fail so signally i 1 Cup competitions. They have not yet lingered either the P.A. or Lancashire Cup, al- though they have twice reached the semi-final for the county trophy. In 1889 they were knocked out by Higher Walton, and now they go down before Bury. We should think Everton regret they did not toss and take the chance of playing on their own field et Anfield-road.

Adversity is a severe lemon. Out Blackburn way they are thankful for small mercies. At the semi-final tie for the Lancashire Cup between, the Rovers and Darwen there were only 5,009 spectators all told, and the bulk of these seemed to come from, the, direction of Barley Bank. Fiva thousand is knything but a pheno- menal gathering, and vet we are told it was far and away the biggest crowd seen at &wood, Park for three tomaths. This is why 5,000 has come to be lboked upon as quite a respectable muster.

div.head: RA.INHILL MURDERS.
div.p: THE RA.INHILL MURDERS.
A WORD IN SEASON BY THE REY: J. YOINGE.

Preaching in Wycliffe Cnurch,. Warrington, on Sunday evening, the Rev. John Tonge took, for hie suhject, "The greatest sight in the world.' His text was, "And all. the multitudes that came together to this sight, when they beheld the things that were done, returned smiting: their breasts.' In the Course of his remarks. he said few things were so popularly attractive as a great sight, and any conspieuous event, such as • ii• public fes- tinity„a splendid pageant, or a royal procession. would collect vast crowds even from remote dis- tances.. Men would undergo much fatigue, incovenience and outlay, in order to see a great shot. There were sights•which were not worth seeing, sights from which right. and true-feeling men would hold back. They had one suck .illustration presented to them even on that very Sabbath day. A quiet villagE not far thence, was being subjected to a renewed invasion from all • directions, simply because it happened to have been the account one of the moot ghostly and . revolting tragedies of modern days. The morbid • and degrading curiosity, which had been and still was im- p•lling thousands of people to see the mere. plaee of a diabolical murder, merited the emphatic protest and the reprof of all right-thinking people. The wise policy wbich some years back put an end to the public execu- tion of criminals should make illegal all public portiayals of evil !leads and should place every possible kindrance in the way of the multitude crowding in morbid curiosity to scenes of infamy and sin. The rush to RainhiliVought to• be frowned upon by Christian public opinion,' even if it could not be stopped by public authority. It was unspeakably indecent and degrading, and investing a diabolical, crime with a notoriety which might lead dis- ordered and disorderly minds to seek to win it for them- selves. Ele should be glad if that public reference from the pulpit awakened discussion upon the matter, and did something towards helping the growth of a pronounced public opinion upon it.
