APPLICATION AT WIDNES FOR A WARRANT.

AT the -Widnes Police Court, on Monday morning, before Mr. J. Biminill and Lieutenant-Colonel an application was made by Mr. Paxton, Liverpool, on behalf of the Public Prosecutor, for a warrant for the apprehension of Frederick B. Deeming, for the murder of his wife and four children at Hainhill. ' The Court was adjourned For an hour, in order to allow Mr. Paxton to read the depositions taken at the inquest to the various witnesses. .

Mter this had been accomplished, Mr. Paxton returned into court,-and said: lam instructed by the Public Prowater to make an application for a warrant for the arrest of Frederick Bayley Deeming, .who is charged with the murder of his wife and four children, at Raiuhill, on the 28th July last year. The application la made under the. Fugitive Offen- ders Act, 1881, under which an offender who is convicted of a crime in England, the punishment for ;which is greater than twelve montheimprisonment with hard labour, is liable to be brought tacit from any one of her Majesty's possessions, and charged with the offence. Your worships will at any rate (now by rumour that a man has been arrested in Australia, and brought to Melbourne, and charged with the murder there. There can be no doubt that this is the same man who is charged with the murders in Rainhill. Of course if he is tried and convicted, the probability is the war- rant Would not he required ; bid in the event, and it appears lobe very unlikely, that he will get Itit there, we will take steps to bring him back to this. country. I have a number of witnesses present who will give a series of facts which will leave do doubt in your worships' minds that Deeming is the man, wanted. Mr. Lewin ' (deputy magistrates clerk),` then read the evidence, as given at. the inquest, of the following persons :—Albert Deeming, fitter, of 55, Canning-st., Birkenhead ; George Pattison, Police Inspector Widnes; Police Sergeant Chi pclutse, Dr. M'Lennon, Widnes ; Mrs. A. Deeming, sister of the deceased ; Mrs. Dove Mathe:, widow, of ; Mrs. Hayes, landlady of Dinham Villa; Mrs. Lally, Henry Short, landlord of the Com- mercial. Hotel, Ha inhill ; Miss Jane Hall, housekeeper at the Commercial Hotel, Miss Barry, barmaid of.the Corn- mercial Hotel; Thomas Duxbury ; Benjamin Young; Walter Hewn, High-street, Present, plasterer ; ' Richard Whitfield Ferguson, goods checker at St. Helens Junction ; and Superintendent Keighley. : Mr. Paxton said, that one of the witnesses, named Richard Hackett, who had been summoned by the police in the same manner as all other witnesses, had not turned tip. As his evidence was very importent, it would he necessary to have him present to swear to his depositions. He therefore applied for a summons to compel Hackett to attend. The summons was granted, and it was then decided 110 adjourn the priteeedintrs until Wednesday morning. Superintendent K iighley informed the Court what the arrangements of the police were with regard to the pre- servation of public order it Rainhill. Mr. Birchall ex- pressed his satisfao!ion, and the Superintendent, then said that before Good Friday there would be nothing left i of Dinham Villa. .

div.head: OPERATI6NB AT THE CAPE.
div.p: OPERATI6NB AT THE CAPE.

Considerable excitement was caused at Capptown by the cablegram from England announcing the, arrest of Deeming on thecharge of havin, murdered his wife at Windsor, near Melbourne, and the statement that the prisoner had visited the Cape. This excitement was re- doubled when it became known that the prisoner had been staving in various, parts of South Africa, for some time, and that he had swindled poonle right and left, also, that durinwhis stay in Johannesburg two. myste- rious murders Were committed there. . _

. It appears that Deeming arrived in Cape Town, with, his wife and three children, in the middle. of 1885, and gave himself out aahavitg come from Australia in search of employment. fle put up at the ralrierston Hotel, and through the instrumentality of the landlord, .obtain- ed a situation as engineer to the city contractors, Deeming remained at his work and gave satisfaction for about nine months, when he had a severe., iilness. He recovered,. and soon afterwards rinwmoced that heR had been appointed manager of the Novitgedacht Gold Company. He wasassisted with funds by friends, and, leaving hilwife at the Palmerston Hotel, proceeded to Johannesburg; Ina very short time Deeming sent down; from Klerkadorp the money necessary to repay the loan., and to pay thwtransport of his wife and family to him..l Only slew weeks after this Deeming himself arrivetli in Cape 'POwn,,accompanied by a broker, and Atated that some English people had given hini wer over £80,000,11 with which he was to speculate in gtulii properties in thel Transvaal. He was very flush of money, and at once I returned to the Transvaal, but a few weeks afterwards he sent hie wife and family to Cape Town, and he, speedily followed himself. He had, vaith him an immense amount of valuable jewellery, and the jewellery. his wife was wearing was itself worth a fortune. Furtheabe had with hirna draft of £2,500, which he banked. Deeming next sent his wife and family to England,and thin re-started swindling operations in Cape town, Kim- berley, Port Elizabeth, and Natal with great success. From. Darixtn. Le•vi, a friend of Deeming's. daswitched the following telegram :—" The poor, boy die& Let all his friends know, but do not e.able this fainily in Eng- land, Rs lam going to take the body home through the Suez- Canal."

-- On Sunday afternoon a sad boating fatality occurred on the Thames, by which Sappers Marshall, Williams, and Fit zzeralcl were drowned. It appears that a party of six engineers stationed at Shormmund Fort; consist- ing of two corporals and four sappers, started on a boating trip to Gravesend, rigging an extempore sail. One of the men's caps blow if into the water, and in endeavouring to secure it the boat c'apsized and the party were thown into the water. The two corporals and one sapper swain ashore, while the other three men were drowned. The bodies of Fitzgerald and Williams have since been recovered.

EAST ER VESTRY MEETINGS.

ilir,—Our vestry meetings being near at hand, may I remind Churchmen of their duty as to our churches be- ing made perfectly free to the people? I think the second Lesson on Sunday evening last ought to convince every Christian that the seating of the people, without any respect of persons, should be the first consideration. Where Our Lord enters the Temple and drives out all that bought and sold, I see no difference between buying aAd selling and hitting and re-letting, or that favourite wystem of appropriation of seats in our places of public 'worship. When will this selfish work cease in our chapels epd churches, and the pure worship in spirit and in truth take its place, so that the Gospel may be preached to the poor as ordtred by our Lord ?—Yours, R. S.

Sir,—Kindly allow me to draw the attention of your readers to these approaching meetings ; each ratepayer is legally entitled to attend. I advise them to procure a copy of a pamphlet on Hymns Ancient and Modern, *4 tested by the Scriptures," W. H. Tucker, price three- pence, to be had from J. Kensit, Paternoster-row, Lon- don. The persons who maintain the use of this book Countenance a sin against God, for the hymns are con- demned in Pros'. 30 c. 6 v. Rev. 2?. c. 1.8 and 19 verses. The burial fees is also a question which needs settling ; many people own graves,non-resident, but once resident. Why should they be charged double if they wish to use Weir own ?—Yours, &c., Frodsham, April 12th, 1892.
ROBERT FOULKES.

HALF-110LIDAY MOVEMENT: PUBLICANS, BARMAIDS, &c. irr,—Publicans, harm lids, wAiters, groomi, and ostlers, &c., are a decent and hardly worked set of people. They seem to be on their legs from early dawn until 10 or 12 o'clock at night both Sundays and week days. Art not these hours sadly too long for their moral

or ph3sical welfare? Brewers who are liberal-minded will, I feel sure, take their hard case into their favourable Consideration. I object to other people enjoying half a bolidAv on Thursdays unless the same benefit be ex- tended to publicans and their people, so as to give the tatter a chance of improving themselves morally and ireligiously as well as physically. The shop men and women seem to be striking for half a Ifoliday on Thursdays. I proposo that the publicans and their people fthould have a similar half-holiday from one p m. on Thursdays until eight a.m. on Fridays. Would not this indulgence probably add ten years to their natural lives? What leisure have they under the present arrangement to attend to their religious 2.oncerns ? These things are of public interest.-1 am, sir, your r hediemt servant, ONE OF THE PUBLIC. 13th April, 1892.

div.head: POLLUTION OF SANKEY 13ILOOK.
div.p: THE POLLUTION OF SANKEY 13ILOOK.

Sif,--ma has beeti my lot to be located for the last five wears on the banks of tha Sankey Brook, anything but a pleasant situation, for at times the stench is intolerable and the colour is anything but that of water. The grey green gives off the most abominable odour, and reaches here on its downward journey from 4 to 6.30 a.m., and the smell is horrible. The black colour Comes next in effi Livia and repulsiveness. Both are very bad, but the first is the worst. There is an Act of Parliament against the pollution of rivers and streams, but as far as Sankey Bridges is concerned it is a dead letter, and the people ate being poisoned because it is not put in force. Middle-aged men tell me that they remember that brook yielding abundance of fedi, and the water could be, and was, used for all d nnestie purposes, except for culinary we. Whit is it now ? Instead of being a pure stream, one of God's precious gifts supplying food to eat and water to drink, it is a noisome poisonous death-dealing sewer. The water in it cannot be used for any known purpose. You cannot feed boilers with it or even cool the still condensers at the chemical works ; and were it riot for floods and spring tides, purifying it to some exteet , life here could not exist. It is a shame, sir, that any man or men should be permitted for a single day to 41eprive a neighbourhood of a pure stream and not only render the water useless, but make it positively danger- • and detritnental to health. I don't know how the people contiguous to the brook keep as well as they do. Perhaps they don't know their danger, and when ill attribute their sickness to some other cause. They com- plain daily, but no one takes any notice, and the nuis- ance increases, growing worse and worse. To whom h• sll we appeal for redress ? There must surely he some itaae responsittle for this state of things, which calls loudly not for abatement but entire prevention.-1 am, sir, yours respectfully, Sankey Bridges, April 11, 1802.
CYMRO.

Sir,—Your readers will doubtless he interested to know the progress that has so far been made ia the proposed Lancashire tribute to Ben Brierley. At a public meeting held in the Mayor's parlour, on March Ist, Alderman Bolin, T. Leech (Mayor of Man- deeter) in the chair, the following resolation, moved by A. Emmott, Esq. (Mayor of Oldham), and seconded by Conncillor Joshua flampson, was carried unanimously : —" That this meeting cordially approves of the sug,ges- Mon that steps should be taken 'Lc) raise at once a fund -sufficient to mark the sense of the high estimation in Wilik:ll Ben Brierley is hell by the people of Lancashire. and which shall serve as a tribute of their respect for him and their admiration for the services which he has rendered to literature."

Mr Brierley is now in his (37th year, and after his re- cent serious indisposition of two years' duration, which Alas resulted in partial paralysis, it is not to be expected that he can do much more work as an author or as a • ,public entertainer. The thousands who have been winused, cheered, and helped by big writings will, it is felt, gladly avail themselves of an opportunity of show- ing their appreciation of this fine exponent of the 'Lancashire character. • Many promises. have been received, and already over "2250 has been paid in to the Hon. Treasurer. These in- -elude subscriptions from the Right Hon. the Earl of J :Derby, KG.; Viscount Cranl)orne, M.P. ; Sir W. 11. lionldsworth, Bart., ; lion. A. . Balfour, ; Sir tl,litred Kay Shut! leaVth, Bart., M.P.; Herbert Phillips, Esq. ; flenjamill Armitage, ; t(Chomlea) ; Robert Leak, Esq., J. M. Maclean, Esq., M.P. ; The Mayors of Manchester, Oldham, and Middleton; Henry Irving, Esq. ; Henry Dunckley, Ksq. ; Frederick Shields, Esq. ; Oeorge :Milner, Esq.. J.P. ; W. E. A. Axon, Esq. ; W. H. Bailey, Esq., : Colonel Le Gereire Starkie ; John Grantham. Esq. ; ThOTIIR9 New- bigging, Esq ; Thomas Kay, Esq. :ri F.: as LinV,Emsl• Henry Slatter, Esq., J.P. ; and Harry Thornber, The subscriptions range from a shilling to ten guineas. $o far the move:milt has been chidly confined to Man- chester, hut it is of course desirable that it shoul.l be ahared in by the whole county and the adjacent portions of Cheshire and Derbyshire, which areso closely identi- fied by industrial and reaidential ties with the district described in Mr. Brierlev's wiitings. The Committee have ventured to ask the Mayors of each Lancashire town to receive subscriptions, and NA, oull be glad to hear from any volunteers to form local committees for the exten- sion of the Fund. We trust that we may count upon your active co-oper- ation in the effort to rOse an amount which shall at least be sufficient to ensure that the remaining years 44 Mr. Brierley and his wife shall he free from anxiety.—Yours truly, •

GREAT LIBERAL MEETING AND OVERFLOW MEETING.

div.head: SPEECHES OP THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE,
div.p: SPEECHES OP THE LIBERAL CANDIDATE,
MR. HERBERT GLADSTONE, &c.

One of the most enthusiastic political gatherings ever seen in W arrington was held in the Public Hall, on Wednesday evening, in promotion of the candi- dature of Dr. Houston the Liberal candidate for the borough. The doors of the hall were opened about seven o'clock and the audience flocked in so rapidly that in a very short space of time the hall was filled in all parts, and all later comers had to be directed to an overflow meeting which it was arranged to hold at the Co-operative Hall in Sankey-street. At the Public Hall—the platform of which wa"s as crowded as was the body of the hall and the gallery —the time was passed in the singing of Liberal and patriotic airs,and at times there were cheers for Mr. Gladstone, Dr. Houston, and others, called for and I given with great enthusiasm. The singing of such songs as " Clear the way for Gladstone's coming," the " Liberal March " and " The Men of ilarlech,"was led by Mr. E. Wright and a small orchestra,and joined in by the audience. On the Chaiyman and principal speakers appearing on the platform there was a loud outburst of cheering. The chair was taken by Mr. J. ylands, President of the Liberal Associa- tion,and amongst those on the plat form, were Mr.H. Gladstone, M.P. Dr. Houston, Q.C., Mrs. Houston, Miss Dutton,the Misses Crosfield,Mrs.Dr.M arkell,the Misses de Beere, Mrs. W. Pierpoint, Mrs. Dr.Gornall, Mrs. Priestman, the Misses Gornall, Mrs. H. Roberts, Mrs. Fleming, the Misses Fleming,Miss Winser, Mrs. G. Blackhurst, the Misses Black h urst, Miss Walker, Mrs. Loughlin, Mrs. G. Clay, Councillors F. A. Roberts, Fleming, Blackhurst, Browne, Bonnell Plumpton, Garner, and Beaman; the Rev. J.' Varley, the Rev. F. K. Freeston ; Messrs. A. H. Crosfield, W. Pierpoint, T. Morris, Dr. Smith, Dr. Gornall, J. S. Garland, R. Garnett, E. J. Guest, C. J. Holmes, T. Birchen, J. Longland, T. B. Kiernan, S. , B. Stringer, S. Kenyon, I'. Caldwell, W. Jeffery, E. ' Wallington, B. Farrar, P. T. Winskill, E. Wal- lington, B. Farrar, W. Hayes, B. Evans, S. Jones, J. Robinson, J. McConville, F. J. Dell, C. H. Knowles, J. E. Warren. J. A. Hayward, G. Holford, D. Dutton, E. Plinston, H. H. Dutton, J. Strange, W. Crosskill, T. B. Malkin, J. Price, A. Benjamitt, J. Mounfield, W. Wright, R. Travis,A. Stirrip, W. Hill, A. H. Dunn, A. Loughlin, Dinwiddie, J. Turton, J. Mercer, T. Clough, A. Corney, W. Wallington, C. Ogden, Wright, D. Clayton, D. Wilcock, T. Cramp- ton, G. Weaver, T. Hayward. R. Roscoe, J. Pod- more, T. Locker, C. Longshaw, G. Ford, J. Evans, W. H. Wallington, J. Harrison (Liverpool), B. Few, J. Pemberton, J. Burgess, A. Silcock, &c. The following apologies for non-attendance had been received. Mr. Z. Armitage, J.P., wrote that it was a matter of regret to him that he was still pre- vented by illness from attending any of the brilli- ant series of meetings which had been held in furtherance of Dr. Houston's candidature, lie trusted that the mass meeting would be as exhila- rating as any that had gone before, and that the result of all their exertions would be to place Dr. Houston at the head of the poll. Mr. Julian Win- ser telegraphiA from Malvern Wells, "Success to the meeting," and Mr. Harold Broadbent wrote from Bala, North Wales, that he was sorry he should not be able to be present at the meeting.

The CHAIRMAN, who was loudly applauded, said he was sorry to announce that one of the speakers whom they expected to have the pleasure of hearing, had been taken ill, and would not be there that night. The Right Hon. S. Walker telegraphed that he had crossed from Dublin to Holyhead, but then felt quite unequal to going on, and therefore very much regretted he could not be present. He (the Chairman), for one, very much re- gretted that Mr. Walker was not able to be present. (Hear, bear.) Some time ago he read a report of a speech by an ex-Mayor of Warrington, in which he spoke of some gentleman having made a very humour- ous speech. In the humourous speech referred to he found it stated that Dr. Houston said a good deal about Home Rule, but if they asked him what he meant by Home Rule he would tell them that he did not know, because Mr. Gladstone hadn't told him yet. (Laughter.) Well, he (the chair- :nan) thought that very humorous indeed. (Laughter.) Then he read some extravagant praise of the present Government, and amongst other things they were cred- ited with was that of being the most constitutional Government they had ever had. It happened that his (the chairman's) idea was, and he thought Dr. Houston being a man of a great deal of legal acumen would bear him out, that the Government was the most con- stitutional government that had existed in his time. (Hear, hear.) He looked for some more humour, but he was bound to say that he was disappointed. He would, however, tell the gentleman he had referred to that Dr. Houston knew perfectly well what Home Rule was, sufficiently at any rate to know what the guiding principles would he. (Hear, hear and applause.) Having condemned the methods of the Government in Ireland, the Chairman went on to say that the demoralisation of ;heir opponents seemed to be something extraordinary. Apparently they were as disorganised as their Government,and that was saying a veld deal. (Hear, hear.) He concluded by saying that he had now better hopes of the Liberals winning War- rington than he had had for a long time, an he should be grievously disappointed if Warrington dill, not ada one to the majority of Mr. Gladstone at the next elec- tion. (Loud cheers.)

div.head: SPEECH OF DR. HOUSTON.
div.p: SPEECH OF DR. HOUSTON.

Dr. llotraron, who had a most enthusiastic greeting on rising, said that magnificent—he thought he might say unprecedented—demonstration augured. well for their success in the struggle in which they were engaged of rescuing this borough from the grasp of the clique that had had a monopoly so long of its representation— (cheers)—and that had used that monopoly in such a way that for the last seven years this great constituency had been practically disfranchised. (Cheers.) In this momentous struggle in which they were engaged, he was glad to think that they had the full sympathy and sup- port of the great Liberal party and of the leaders of that party. (Hear, hear.) Night after night, there had stood beside him, on the platforms of the town, staunch mem- bers of that party, members of Parliament and others, and that night they had amongst them the worthy son of the venerable and illustrious leader of the party. (Prolonged cheers. A call for " Another for his father" was heartily responded to. They should have hid also with them the first law officer of /ler Majesty's Govern- ment in Ireland during Mr. Gladstone's last administra- tion, but illness had overtaken him ; and after making an effort to reach Warrington, he was obliged to return to Ireland. But at some future time, tie hoped not far distant, they would have an opportunity of listening to his great eloquence, and of getting the benefit of the great information he possessed on the question of the day. (Hear, hear.) Now, they ought to derive great hope and encouragement from the sympathy and sup- port they had so received,and it ought to ani tnate them to more vigorous exertions—if any stimulus were wanted to make those exertions more vigorous than they have been. For his part he could scarcely believe that any such stimulus was wanted. The efforts that ha 4 been made by those gentlemen who had been managing this long campaign of his in Warrington had been beyond all praise. ,(Cheers.) And night after night CBOWDED AUDIENCES HAD ASSEMBLED

and had listened with admirable patience and admirable attention to the exposition of his views and of the ouier speakers upon the great questions of the day. From what he had observed of the spirit in which the speeches were received, he had been able to gauge the breadth and depth of the Liberalism of Warrington, and he was satisfied that it had the true Radical and democratic ring. (Cheers.) He hoped he was not over sanguine in believ- ing this, that there were many people in Warring- ton who, though not calling themselves Liberals, were yet satisfied in their own minds that the only way to redress the wrongs of Ireland and the grievances under which the working-men and others were now labouring was to pat a Liberal .Government into power. (Cheers.) The people of Warrington were too clear-sighted not to see through PRETRNSIONS OF TILE TORY AND UNIONIST PARTY that they had brought peace and prosperity to Ireland ; and they were also too clear-sighted to be taken in by boasts of the Tory party that they were the friends of the workingmen. (Hear, hear.) The people distrusted the policy of the Tory party in both these departments, and if they wanted a clue to the spirit of the policy of the Tory party in Ireland. the clue would be afforded by the convention which the members of the Tory Unionist party proposed:to hold in Ulster. They were en- gaging at the present time in their old policy,and a ph icy which was congenial to their spirit, the policy of raking up and rekindling the einbers of religious animosity be- tween the two parties in Ireland. (Hear, hear.) 'hey i were engaged n a conspiracy against the peace, and a plot against the unity of Ireland. (" Shame.") It appeared that they had come to the conclusion that they would not have anything to do with the Parliament that was to tie established in Dublin by a law to Kt passed by the Imperial Parliament in this country. With smooth pretensions on their tongue of loyalty to the Crown and with pretensions of the veneration in which they held the Imperial Parliament, they would Mt them beforehand that they weiuld disobey the law which had received the royal a.sent, and that they would repudiate the authority of the Imperial Parliament. They told them that they would not present themselves for election, much leas vote in the

(" What a pity -;-5 ---(Laughter.) They had passed, or intended to pass a self-denying ordinance. (Laugh- ter.) They had ha/ self-denying ordinances before this, but their history had not been very encouraging. (Hear, hear.) They were ordinances based upon good if mistaken motives, but what was the mltiTris with which these gentlemen proposed to pass this ordinance ? The motive they had in their hearts was to create dis- sension and difference between the nerth and south of Ireland. (" They wont do it.") They would not suc- ceed. (Cheers.) He thought the notion of these gentlemen of abstaining from attendance in a Dublin Parliament and thinking that by so doing Ulster would be enriched was simply the most absurd and ridiculous idea that ever entered into man's head. It appeared that Colonel Saunderson I was going to sulk in a Primrose Habitation. (Laughter.) He thought Ireland could manage to rub on pretty well without Mr. T. R. Russell (laughter) and he thought they would manage to survive the loss of Mr. Johnson, of Ballykilbeg. (Laughter.) And if they should be deprived of the great services of the other dead-heads they must put up with the loss of tbem also. (Laughter.) The people distrusted the Tory policy in Ireland ; they certainly were not satisfied with the policy of the present Government towards working-men : they did not believe in the measures they passed. He would tell them why. The measures passed by the present Tory Government when they had anything of a Liberal complexion at all were

or Guardians elections. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) They must abolish the property qualification, and they must adopt the principle of the ballot both in Local Board and Guardians elections. (Cheers.) Fourthly, they were pledged to the cheapening of elections in order to allow men whe are not blessed with much wealth tip stand for Parliament if their qualifications are sufEcient. (Cheers.) And in the fifth place a democratic Govern- ment would

the same as now. It would be a far worse state of things If England rejected the constitational solution of the question, and constitutional methods were exhausted, they would have to face once more the fell and hideous condition of

REBELLIOI7S AND BLOOD-STAINED IRELAND ; ' and so the wretched business would go on. He did not believe it was necessary to put these gloomy anticipa- tions before them. (Applause.) Everything that had happenel went to show that tha feeling in this country was steady and strong in the Home Rule direction. The Irish people had been waiting for six years, confident in the belief that England Would at last awake to their needs and determine to do them justice. He did not appeal to the electors on false issues, but asked them merely to give their best attention to the subject, to weigh the issue, and consider what was best, and when the time of the general election came go to the poll and vote as their consciences told them • and if they cild that, he had no doubt of the result. (Loud and continuous cheering.)

- Mr. £.'H. CROSFIELD who was cordially received,. in proposing a vote of thanks to the Chairman and speakers, said he hoped Mr. Gladstone had had ocular and aural evidence that night that his efforts had been far from wasted in Warrington. (Cheers.) Referring to the obstacles which were thrown in the road of progress by the inertia and selfishness of Toryism, Mr: Crosfield said. they should not accept the invariable ""No " of the Tories, but they shoold continue constantly and earnestly to strive and fight for the principles and the conditions under which men not only had more opportunity for wider interests and healthier delights in lite, but also more readiness to grasp and capacity to use them. (Cheers.) In Warrington the Liberals : had a candidate who by his unfailing courtesy to his opponents, by his kindly humour, and by his marked intellectual power and grasp of every question I he had dealt with, was entitled to, and, he believed, had won, their genuine respect and esteem. (Cheers.) In the minds of many of them there was constantly pre- sent too the thought of their marvellous old leader— (cheers)---who in his old age,stin "scorned delights and lived laborious days,' and of whom he had heard it eloquently said he was to the youngest of them an in- spiration and to the oldest an example. (Cheers.) The opportunity, the golden moment, would soon be upon them, and lie thought if they were worthy of the cause of Liberalism they would then help to swell that historic and momentous victory, which, as one of its chief con- sequences, would give the final overthrow of that ancient and false image of coercion, with its front of brass and Its feet of clay, which shalt then be tumbled in the dust. (Loud cheers.)

s Mr. W. PIERPOINT, in seconding the proposal, said he did not intend to delay the meeting, but in response to loud cries or" go on," he added that they had done some- thing to revive the old dog of Liberalism in Warrington, and theiropponents,who had reproached them with being bankrupt in purse and bankrupt in, principle, would find that the old animal had been regenerated and that his teeth were exceedingly sharp. All that they would find to their cost when Dr. Houston became member for Warrington, (Loud cheers.) What they had done they had done in the best interests of their community and of the country at large,. and he could pledge himself, and he thought he could pledge their honoured Chairman, that they would, leave no stone un- turned to achieve that SUCCPSi they SAW looming in their immediate future. (Cheers.) Having expressed his pleasure at seeing many ladies present, he asked them to do all they could to help Dr,. Houston, because the Liberalsidid not wantlto win this time by 529, but by a majority exceeding a thousand. (Laughter and cheers.) He would tell them why—bscause the Tories had volunteered the statement that they had broken the neck of the Liberal party. Such. statements had been proved to be untrue, and he wanted the working-men of Warrington to give such a majority. to Dr. Houston as would break the neck of the Tory party of the borough. (Loud cheem) The resolution was then put to the meeting, and car- ried with accclamation. The Chairman having res- ponded, the meeting terminate&
CROWDED OVERFLOW MEETING.
EMIT usrAsnc PROCEEDINGS.

An overflow meeting for those who were crowded out of the Public Hall, w es held in. the Ce-eperative Sankey-st. This hall was also rapidly filled, and became so crowded that many were unable to ,obtain admittance. Mr. W. Pierpoint presided, and there were also on the platform Dr. and Mrs. Himecon, Mr. Hi Gladstone, M P. 9 Councillors H. Roberts, Fleming. Beaman, and Flood, Messrs. .1. C. Holmes, Dunbobbin, John, Price, and J. Clayton (agent). The CHURNIAN expressed the regret that the Public Hall was not larger so that it could have held those pre- sent. There was no d 3 übt considerable disappointment among them at not being at the larger meeting. There vras a great amount of enthusiasm, among the Liberals in Warrin,gton,greater,he thought,even than in 1830. Mr. Pierpoint then proceeded to deal with some items of the Liberal programme. Referring to the Home Rule question, he said most people, would say that was the great question before the country. He agreed.with them,, and he was perfectly satisfied that mail they had settled that in a manner satisfactory to them and the Irish, people they could have no possible getting.on with matters of labour legislation. He thought the question of Home Rule had really been taken out of the region, of discussion on public platforms. The electors had declared in an un- mistakable manner that Home Rule was a question that must be dealt with, and he thought. it was quite time it was taken from the public platform . and returned to the House of Representativeseand there was no doubt that when the general election came there would be a very large majority. indeed of Lib 'rids returned mainly ou the question of Home Rule for Ireland. The great question that would have to be settled after that was the question of electoral reform—so that a man might be placed on, the register and kept there, and that every means should be devised whereby every citizen of this country who was entitled toa vote should be put upon the list without any necessity for his attend- ing the revision court,, and without the thousand and one objections raised.by one party or the other. At the present moment every difficulty was thrown in the way of the working-man getting a vote, whereas every oppor- tunity should be afforded himfor'getting his name, on the register as early as possible and, keeping it there,because the mere fact of a man moving from one town to another ought not to disenfranchise him as at present. (Ap- plause.) Councillor Pierpoint detailed a case in point, that of a friend of his at Latchford, who, he said, lost his vote in Warrington through removal to another town, and would have to wait till 18941 before he was qualified there. (Councillor Fleming: Shame.) Shorter Parliaments were another reform, that was necessary. It was all very well to talk about a seven years Parliament causing more prosperity or less disturbance in the country. He found that the mere fact of.a disso- lution geing to take place was interfering with his trade. People said they wanted to. know what was going to be the effect of the general election before they went largely into trade. That was one way of looking at the matter, but the real way to look at it was that the electors, if a Parliament did not last so long would be able to deal bet- ter with members who did not do their duties and did not attend at all (A voice from. the platform : " Sir Gilbert Greenall,7 and applause.), If a man who took his seat in the House of Commons was not able to fulfil his duties to the electorate he ought in common honesty to resign, so that they might elect somebody who would attend bet- ter. The next question dealt with by the speaker was the payment of members. He thought the time had arrived when that would have to be taken into consideration. The Tory candidate for the borough gaee utterance to a remark as.to,the payment of members which aroused in his breast when he read it a feeling of very great indig-. nation. He made the observation that a lot of men who were too idle to work and too proud to beg—a_ very good dentition of a cornerm an—would be just the kind of men to set up to. represent constituencies in the House of Commons. He. endorsed the opinion of Mr, Henry Roberta that such an utterance ought to impress the working-men of Warrington with the conviction that the Tory candidate for the boron gh was not at all a fit represemative for them. (Cheers.) The speaker referred to the large salaries paid to the various officials of the Government and the Court, pointing,out the uselessness of some of the latter functionaries,, and remarking that this class. of people were those who cried the loudest against payment of members. In drawing to a close he observed that he was coining very much, to , the opinion that the whole of the working-men of, War- rington were coming over to the Liberal side—(cleeers)— and he was satisfied from the audiences they had had, at the series of receptions that at all events their meetings, had been Med witn, respectable, decent, well-behaved, honest, sound Liberal werking-men politicians. He exo pressed the opinion that if the electors would only make up. their minds that this fight on behalf of the candida, furs of Dr. Houston was more theirs than hisethe result would: be a triumph for Liberal principles. (Cheers.) MTS. Houston then sang "Come live in my heart and. pay no rent," and as an encore " What Paddy gave the drum," and added two verses referring to the local con- test, which were loudly cheered. Councillor Fawn then addressed the meeting,. and said the present Government had not paAsed one com- plete measure that would satisfy the Labour party. There had never been so many Labour struggles as during the last six years, awl they were not to be satiso fied by Commissions or knocking people's brains out at Trafalgar-square. (Applause.) At this point Councillor I.J. Roberts took the chair in the place of Mr. Pierpoint. Dr. HOUSTON, who was received with load cheers, next spoke. He expressed his regret that there was not a larger hall in Warrington to accommodate the electors ; and urged upon then to work their hardest in the present election, The Tories, he said, had played their last card, Mr. Goschen'e budget, and that had not turned out a trump. He drew from this the conclusion that the election might be smolt us at any moment. He did not think the Goverment could hold together and postpone the evil day un as they might the dissolution must come at a .very early date. The Tories were at present, erevassing. and working hard, and it behoved

every Liberal to dos° also. The election would without doubt he upon thew very soon, and so they ought to be lin readiness. (Cheers.) Councillor Roberts and Messrs, Benjamin Price, and Maseden also spoke. Mt. Haaraint GLAnsTotrif then addressed the meeting. He fold that this overflow meeting aftgured wall for the election. Dr. Houston deserved the support of the Liberal party. Lancashire had done Well from Btirnley to Rosseridale. He also believed that Cheshire wovid do the same. They were going to win Cheater, and there ought to be a match between Chester and Warrington which should have the largest Liberal majority. le showed how the Tory bad tried to create good trade spending great sums of money on military and naval', objects, and that now they had got through Cieir spencl-j ing we were experiencing the normal condition of trade! under Tory rule. He also referred to the representation of labour and said when it was more in touch with the House of Commons, the tatter would be able te deal better with the liouseof Lords. (Cheere.) . .
A vote of thanks to Mr. Gladstone &LIS 'the chairmen clbsed the proceE,dings.

div.head: NOT RONEST MEASURES.
div.p: NOT RONEST MEASURES.

(Hear, hear.) They were not genuine metal ; they were pinchbeck, made for show and not use. (Laughter and cheers.) They kept the word of promise to the ear but they broke it to the hope. (Hoar, hear.) They had only to consider for a moment some of the measures that they had passed, and in this respect the measures they had passed for Ireland and the measures that they had passed for England were exactly of a piece. Take the Land Purchase Bill for Ireland. Like all other cases in which these quasi-Liberal measures were passed by a Tory Government, they were invariably passed after they had been steeped to the lips in pledges not to admit the principle of such measures at all. (flear,hear.) They always began by deluding their own party, and when they had succeeded in that, they proceeded to jockey the country. (Hear, hear.) The Land Purchase Bill was an instance of that policy. They began by pro- testing that they would not give one farthing of the tax- payers' money or pledge one atom of the country's credit for the purpose of buying out the landlords ; and, upon that as one plank of their platform, they got into power. (Hear, hear.) Then they proceeded to swallow all their own words, and brought in a measure of land purchase. The next step was reached when the measure, about which there had been so much boasting' turned out to be a sham. It was perfectly unworkable. What was intended to be, or expected to be, a panacea for some of the evils in Ireland had turned out to be a piece of pure political quackery. (Cheers.) It was the same with the Irish Local Government Bill. That was to be a masterpiece of their legislation; that was the Bill that was to have put an end to the discontent in Ireland, and to have silenced the demand for Home Rule. They had produced their Local Government Bill, and it was received with merited derision and indignation because it turned out to be a tissue of buffoonery flavoured with Balfourian insolence. (Cheers.) Turning from Irish to English measures, take the Allotment legislation that was in- tended and would have been a great boon both to the toilers in the country and toilers in the towns, because by providing a happy and comfortable home for the man who lived in the country, it would enable him to remain there and would have diverted from the towns, that current of labour population which was swamping the labour in the towns. (Hear, hear.) But this allotment legislation had one fatal defect, namely, it wanted that popular control which was necessary to give it vitality, and the result was that the allotment legislation had been practically a dead letter up to the present day. (Cheers.) Then again, the measure introduced for the purpose of creating small holdings, was destined to fall stillborn upon the country, despite the warning of people who understood tha subject, because the only thing that could give it life and vitality was the right and - -

POWER OF COMPULSORY PURCHASE. (Cheers.) What state did ney think the railways would be iu at the present day if they rested upon the mutual agreement between landlords and the railway companies —if the legislature had completely confirmed the prin- ciple that the rights of property were not subordinate to the public interest ? Why, they might be in the era of stage coach and wagons instead of goods trains and limited mails. (Cheers.) These were merely illustra- tions of the vital and inherent defects of Tory legislation. These were the dividends as they had been described —(laughter)—the dividends of that bubble company of which Mr. Balfour was one of the managing directors—(laughter)—dividends which lie ventured to say did not increase the income of the shareholders, but ruined the credit of the concerh, and would lead to its being final'y wound up. (Laughter.) The country was

TIRED OF SIUM LICGIALATION. The people had got a sturdy political appetite, and they wanted substantial poll 'feat food. They would not be contented with the light refreshment--(laughter)—the airy delicacies and ornamental confectionery that were cooked in Primrose. Rabitations—(laughter)—and served out by dames and ruling councillors. (Renewed laugh- ter.) They wanted substantial viands, and they knew where to go to get them. The market would soon be open—(cheers)---and everybody who had a voting paper would have a ticket with which he could buy in the market. (Loud cheers.) MR. FIERBER I' GLADSTONE'S SPEECH.

Mr, HERBERT GLADSTONE, M.P., on rising to sneak was greeted with loud and continued applause, and rounds of cheering for" his rather" and "his mother" were also given. He SAid that Dr. Ilmston had gone to an overflow meeting which, they were informed, was crammed. He thought they had all the Liberals in Warrington in that hall, but he was glad to hear that there were plenty more outside. (Hear, hear.) The prospect of freeing their horaugh from the Tory domina- tion which had hung over it for so many years was brightening every day, and he trusted that under the brilliant leadership of their gallant candidate they would win a great victory at the general election. (Hear, hear and lend cheers.) It was not for him to say any- thing to them in

RECOMMENDATION OF DR. HOUST3N. He was a man distinguished by his ability and by his learning, and excellent as were those qualifications he had something which was higher—he was distinguished by his unswerving fidelity to political principle. (Cheers.) As an Englishman he was fond of fair play, but•in one respect the conditions of fair pity were wanting in that contest. There was a champion on the Conservative side, but on the Liberal side thay had two, and in the gracious lady—(cheers)—who had just left the hall (for the overflow meeting) their candidate had one who would give him valuable and material assistance in fight- ing and winning that constituency. (Loud Cheers.) They would shortly be called upon to make their choice between two great political parties. He would say if he could between TWO 0 RRAT POLITICAL PROGRAMMRS.

But what was the Conservative programme? He did not know what it was and had never heard of it. (Hear hear.) Their one policy at the present moment was to oppose the Liberal programme, but they had none of their own. Why should they ? The country would not believe them if they did produce a programme. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Coming along that evening in the train he read in a newspaper of a poor man, who was, he was afraid, at that moment dying in a hospital in New York. He was known out there as the " human ostrich," because for the last six years having Seen employed in appearing at meetings and swallowing tin tacks, ten- penny nails, bits of crockery and bite of glass, but re- cently he took a pint pot full of the commodities he had mentioned and they proved too much even for his hard- ened digestion. (Laughter.) In the Tory party they had the political ostrich—(Cheers and laughter)—a party fed by its Government on everything they would have thought distasteful and abhorrent to it during the last six years. But what was the result ? Even the tough digestion of the Tory party throughout the country was getting tired of the food given to it, and they had "Weil constituency after constituency revolt against the policy of the present Government. (Cheers.) But the Liberals had a political programme. They had adopted what was known as

div.head: NEWCASTLE PILOGRAMME
div.p: THE NEWCASTLE PILOGRAMME

and which Dr. Houston had adopted. (Cheers.) That programme was assailed on two sides. It was- assailed to someextent by leaders of the democracy and of labour who say that it did not go far enough. On the other side the Tories told them they were promising everything, and that the Newcastle programme included everything. Let them consider the programme from those two points of view. He had no doubt there were some there that night who thought that that programme was not democratic enough. These he asked to assume that a Government was returned to power dominated by labour influences, and then ask themselves what under : the present political conditions were the measures which such a Government, in order to retain its democratic supporters, must inevitably pass. (Cheers.) First of all, they would deal with

div.head: •PAYMENT Or MEMBERS.
div.p: •PAYMENT Or MEMBERS.

(Cheers.) He did nOCs;ty-iha-t-;.-I..Tberal Governtnent would deal with payment of members in the first, the second, or the third years of office, but he did say that the Liberal party was pledged to the adoption of the principle. Secondly, a democratic Government would pass a STRONG REGISTRATION BILL.

(Ches.) They knew ii.Y-a-b-n-k.i-t—tlio---re-g.istration diffi- culty. so did he.. Perhaps his own constituents were even greater sufferers than they in Warrington owing to the present ridiculous state of the laws. In the third place a democratic Government would have to deal with plural voting and brinz in

div.head: ONE MAN ONE VOTE.'
div.p: ONE MAN ONE VOTE.'
(Cheers.) A Liberal Government ;;as pledged t,) put that in the very forefront of its lislation, and in deal- ing with that they must not neglect either Local Board

div.head: 9110 RTEIf PARLIAMENT
div.p: 9110 RTEIf PARLIAMENT

(Cheers)—and to that also the Liberal party was pledged. There they had five first-class measures to which a Government, however popular and however democratic, it might be, must first direct its attention, and to those measures the Liberal party was pledged. I (Cheers.) Having referred to some of the measures ' which the Tory Government had formulated under the pressure of the agricultural vote, Mr. Glad- stone 'alluded to the recent Progressive victory in London, and said that they had even- reason to believe that London as well as Lancashire would return a sub- stantial Liberal majority at the next general election. He had been criticised for saying at a meeting in London that if the Liberal party had made mistakes at all it was that they had already put forward rather more measures than they would probably be able to get through in four years. He had not said that the attention of the Liberal party wwild be limited to the two great measures of Home Rule for Ireland and Home Rule for London. Everybody knew that the House of Commons did net deal with one measure alone in a session. Every year that passed a great number of Acts were added to the statute book, and let him submit to them some kind of a test of the capacity of the next Liberal Government— assuming it to be a large majority—in the way of legis- lation. Take the LIBERAL Goveßwmmer or, 1869

and mark wl-1;t- it did in its first four ye;;; of office. It passed the Irish Church Act—(cheers)—the Irish Land Act,the National Education Act,the Ballot Act—(cheers) —the Act for the abolition of purchase in the army —(cheers)—and the Act for the abolition of tests at the Universities. (Hear, hear.) He thought, therefore, that they might fairly say that in four years of the

NEXT LIBERAL GOVERNMENT, assuming it had a sufficient working majority, they could pass six measures which would be equivalent to those he had named. (Cheers.) Opposite the Irish Church Act he put the Home Rule Bill for Ireland— (cheers) ; opposite the Irish Land Act the London Gov- ernment questiou—(cheers) ;—opposite national educa- tion he put a large measure dealing with County Govern- ment questions, which should include the setting up of parish and district councils, a fuller measure with regard to allotments and small holdings, and the giving to the local authorities of the direct veto in regard to the liquor traffic—(cheers) ;—against the Ballot Act he put a comprehensive bill dealing with the question of registration, one man one vote, and the abolition of the ' returning officers' fees as far as candidates were con- cerned—(cheers) ;—beside the abolition of pdrchase in the army he put the question of payment of members— (cheers)—and opposite the abolition of University tests he put the disestablishment of the Welsh Church. —(Cheers.) In that estimate he made no calculation for the effects of passing Home Rule. He had gone into that matter very closely, and he believed that if they transferred the purely Irish business from Westminster to Dublin they would save something like 25 per cent, of the time of the House of Commons. ,Cheers.) One sentence in the speoch he made in London had been very much laid hold of by some of the Irish papers, and that was when he said that, for his own part, he sin- cerely hoped no member of ' the Liberal party would place London behind Ireland in the importance of the measure which was necessary for its good government. The Home Rule question stood distinctly first, and it was an imperial question in the highest sense of the word, but Ireland had been relieved to some extent by the land legislation which had been passed. 20 or 30 per cent, for rents had been transferred from landlords to tenants, and that had brought a great relief to the poormt classes in Ireland. He spoke, therefore, for the social condition of Ireland as it was now, and they looked to London as it was now, and knowing London as he did from north to south and from east to west, he said that the condition of the POOR PEOPLE IN LONDON

appealed more to one's heart and one's sympathies by the very wretchedness and misery of a great deal of it than did even the condition of the Irish people. He did not minimise the necessities of Ireland, but he did not want to minimise the necessities of Londoners. (Hear, hear.) If the people of London demanded, as he be- lieved they would, that we should give them Horne Rule and relieve them from the incubus of the many inte- rests which had fastened on their vitals, and give them powers which Warrington had had for many years, but which they had never had ; then it would be the duty of the English people cheerfully to acquiesce in the Government dealing effectually with the question. (Cheers.) Reverting to the Irish question. Mr. Gladstone said the Tories were organising themselves in opposi- tion, and once more endeavouring

TO PLAY UPON THEIR FEARS, They were always so anxious, so timid, so fearful. There were vine people who delighted in being miserable and conjuring up unnecessary fears He once heard of two elderly spinsters upon whom a friend called, who found them looking exceedingly miserable, and who on his ask- ing why said they had just been thinking if they had both mauled, and one of them had had a son and the other a daughter and they had married and had a baby and the baby died what a sad thing. (Loud laughter and cheers—A Voice : " You are a chip of the old block.") When he read the speeches of the Tories he was reminded of these two elderly spinstels : their fears were unneces- sary. The Liberals had driven a good many of them out of sightoix years ago when they fought the battle of Home Rule,and were beaten. There were many and grave ob- jections which they had to face then,but which they hal not got to face now. Six years ago the Tories played on their fears because of the land question. Mr. Balfour's Land Purchase Bill enabled the landlords to sell their estates if they were frightened, so Home Rulers need not trouble themselves about them. They had this golden bridge, and could -walk over it if they liked. In the next place the cry of separation was raised because it was proposed in the bill as it stood to take the Irish representation away from Westminster. The Liberal leaders would pledge themselves to retain Irian representation in due proportion at Westminster ; and as long as that was done you had a solid and tangible proof that no separation was intended. The third fear which was conjured up was that the strong phalanx of 85 nationalists in Parliament would, if Home Rule were conceded, ride over Ireland, as they would ride over the House of Commons if they could. But they were banded together by one political issue, the issue of Home Rule, and when you gave scope to their energy and ability in Dublin,natural influences would reassert them- selves ; they would fall into parties, and you would get the play of parties in Ireland as you had it in Englaad. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) He regretted

TUN SPLIT IN THE NATIONALIST PARTY but it had had one excellent effect. It had had a power- ful influence on the Ulster mind, for the people of Ire- land, the loyal minority in particular, saw that they would not be exposed to the domination of one party, that the Irish question had produced a distinct division of opinion among them, and they knew perfectly well that every Irish question that came up in the Dublin Parliament would produce like effects, resolving the whole nationalist party into its natural elements in its own country. (Cheers.) There was.still the old bogey of Ulster They saw now that the leaders of the Orange party, including even a inomner or tier Majesty's G-Jverriment, were bandinif themselves together in order to resist Home Rule. The opponents of Home Ruh, were always asking what some Rule was, but they seemed to know what it was; since they said they were going to resist it; and what was the use of organis- ing to fight against you snow not what? (Laughter and cheers.) Well, they had got to Seal with this Ulster question. Ulster was the wrong ward. rhe Ulster majority probably was Catholic and Nationalist ; it was mercy a north-east corner of Ireland which was so desperately opposed to Home Rule ; and it was this north-eastern corner of Ireland which was opposing its will to that of the rest of Ireland,and of the great major- ity of the people in England, Wales, mad otlaml, and more than that, the opinion of the great colonies of our Empire. (Cheers.) Let them band themselves together when they liked. Let Colonel Saunderson and Mr. T. W. Russell put themselves at the head of their merry men in the north-east of Ireland ; and they would hare Mr. Balfour's Coercion. Act handy to shut them up. (Loud taught& and cheers.) If. that Act was good for the majority of the Irish people, vrhy then if the minority deserved should they not have it ? (Chum.) Let the Government say they approved of this movement or net. If they did not let them put their foot down and deal with the matter—(cheem)—and if they did, then let Lord Salisbury,Mr. Arthur Halfour,and Colonel Saunder- son put on the red cap of revolution themselves and go and

div.head: LEAD VIE OMANGENIME TO THEIR DOOM.
div.p: LEAD VIE OMANGENIME TO THEIR DOOM.

(Cheers.)Hescanting on the manner in which the Govern- ment had falsified their pledges to Ireland, the speaker said the fact that they delayed their Local Government Bill till their last year of office was a strong indication of their wish not to pass the Bill at all. They could have passed it if they liked. As to Mr. Chapliu's Allot- ments and Small' Holdings Bill, there was not, he be- lievecLa single'Consetvative candidate who in 1888 spoke in favour of such a measure. Mr. Chaplin himself was opposed to it entil the success of the agricultural labourer's conference in London and the long series of reverses 'in county elections were seen. (Cheers.) If the Governmentwere honest men, which however, he very much doubted,—(laughter)—then at the eleventh hour they .could make a successful effort to pass this Bill into law. This bill and other work the Government had in hand which had also precedence over the Irish I Bill, made, It absolutely impossible for the Irish Bill to pass. And if they could not pass it now they would never pass it next yeah Practically the bill was dead and gone, and he charged the Tory Government with wilfully misleading and deliberately postponing the bring- ing in of this bill to the sixth session, in order that they might with the greatest care shelve it.. Their Irish policy had been revealed in ,all its nakedness—not local self-government but perhaps coercion, and plenty of it. If unhappily it was to be coercion instead of Home Rule still, he could not say,' that six years hence it Vnuld be

THE. SHIP CANAL
A COMTANY'S HOPPER SUNK.

The Manchester Ship. Canal Cotnnany's hopper No. 3, when coming.up the Mersey at ten o'clock on Tuesday night, collided with tho- steamer Armathvvaite, inward bowl° from Messina., which was at anchor. Ccaoider- able damage was done to the steamer. After getting clear of the Armathwaitw the hopper proceeded ep the Mersey, endeavouring to reach ths Canal. but sank when close to the school ship, Conway. The crew were res- cued and landed at the Prince's Landing Stage.

div.head: CONTRe.CT. FaEt SECOND SECTION.
div.p: CONTRe.CT. FaEt SECOND SECTION.

The contract for completing the second of the four secttonsinto whielvtfre line.of canal between Manches- ter and Runcorn- has been divided has been secured by Messrs. Whittaker Brothers, Limited, of Leeds. The two remaining sections will be let probably within another month, and shortly afterwards an authoritative state- ment will be made in regard to the cost of completing the entire undertaking. On the waterway new open, between Eastliam and the river Weaver, the traTat is being dealt with in awry satisfactory way. On liatur- day forenoon the steamship Rosalind, with 850 tons of cement, entered the canal from the Mersey, and the cargo was discharged at a tempqrary wharf in the Weaver Pool in the course of 18 working hours. A per- manent wharf is in course of construction at this, point, at which it will, he possible to unload half-a-dozen vessels at one time: This wharf will be comploted in thecourse of another month.

div.head: IMPORTANT DRYELOPMENT AT RUNCORN:.
div.p: IMPORTANT DRYELOPMENT AT RUNCORN:.

Information has reached the authorities at Runcorn that the. directors ~4f the Manchester Ship Canal Company have recommended to the executive committee the pro- vision of a lay-by, measuring 600 feet long, and to the depth ,of 26 feet, with a jetty or wharf for the use of vessels of large burden. Its proposed situation is oppos- ite the present docks, and its construction is to be contemporaneous with the making of the canal. This development is hailed with satisfaction by the inhabitants of the town, as it is sure to be a source of commercial benefit to the,district. The lay-by will provide accom- modation for vesselsJrorn foreign parts of 2.ooo'cr 3,000 tons burden breaking bulk and reloading at Runcorn, in place of stopping at other ports. The great importance of this lay-by may:be estimated by the feet that the sill of the tidal basin of Runcorn Docks is 14 feet higher than the level of this canal, which altogether excludes vessels of deep draught from the port, and the proposed lay-by will' be an efficient substitute for a deep dock,and,mill .of the utmost beneftt. It has been mooted-by practi- cal men well acqpainted with ships and trada that the lay-by ought to be at least 800 feet long, but no doubt tlei Commissioners will give the subject the fullest con- sideration u all • i tis hearings.

Afire occurred on Tuesday night at Scott and Sorls Wool Store,. Dumfries. The damage is .estimated at /10,000 d A serious outbroek of foot-and-mouth disease has oc- curred at Woodstock-park, Sittingbourne,, flock of .400 sheep anddamba being affected. Two little daughters of a miner named-flerringtos, of Rothwell,,nearLeeds, have been poisoned by. takinjonice. Powder during their mother's aysence. A man named Mulraney was killed in a coalpit at Tylde.sley on. Suturday, and another named Sidlow terribly injured by the explosion of a slant. Whilst a girl named Jefferson ,was attemptin* to enter a train in motion at Newport Pagnell, on Wed.nes- day morning, she slipped between- the eartiage. and; the ' platforsia, and was killed. ' Thomas Watson was killed ca M.ondLy and: serious injury caused to another named Samuel banks, at the Tantany Pit, Rill End Colliery,,West Broanwich„by a. fall of coal, under which both were buried.

On Saturday night a Mail natne-d— Henry Richards quarrelled with another named Lewis HamiUna at Meat:sham, near Trowbridge, and fatally shot him with a revolver. The murderer is at largo. Mrs. Darbyshire and Mrs. Davies ware on Monday among the successful candidates elected,as guardians for Hove in the Steyning Union. This is the Arst time that ladies have been elected to this board. Sir William, Harcourt, replying to a Derby- correspom• dent, says hohas long had under consideration the means of restraining the indiscriminate sale and possession of &rearms, bla practical difficulties, have been found very great. The University Boat Race was towed on Saturday, and in the result Oxford won by two lengths and a quarter. The time was 19rain. 2Lsec.„ much the fastest :in which the race la as ever been rowed. The nex4:, best is slower by 14 seconds. Captain Middleton while ridincz in the Midland Sports- man's Race in connection with the House of Commons Meeting at Kineton, on Saturday, was violently thrown, owing to his horse stumbling, and was instantaneously killed, his neck being broken, Another Anarchist outrage is ruir.:et.l from France, an infernal machine exploding on Sunday on the window sill of a house occupied by a magistrate at compiegne. The window was blown to pieces. Several further nu- portaut arrett9 of Anarohists have:been made in Spain.

SALKELD, Secretary of the Runcorn Burial Board. April, 13th, 1892.
